Baku is long attested under the Perso-Arabic name بَاکُو (bākū). Early Perso-Arabic sources also referred to the city as بَاکُوه (bākūh) and بَاکُویَه (bākūya), all of which seem to come from a Persian name. Further etymology is unknown.
A popular etymology in the 19th century considered it to be derived from Persian بَادْکوبَه (bādkōba, “wind-pounded”), compound of بَاد (bād) + کوب (kōb) + ـَه (-a). This etymology was first proposed in the 17th century-chronicle Tārīkh-i ʕālam-ārā-yi ʕabbāsī.
Another and even less probable etymology explains the name as deriving from Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (*bgkwdk' /⁠*baykōyōē, *bakkōyōē⁠/), an unattested compound of [Book Pahlavi needed] (bg /⁠bay, bag⁠/, “God; lord”) + [Book Pahlavi needed] (kwd /⁠kōy⁠/, “street, lane”) + [Book Pahlavi needed] (-wyk' /⁠-ōē⁠/), meaning "God's town". It may be compared with Baghdād ("God-given") in which dād is the Old Persian word for "give".
During Soviet rule, the city was spelled in Cyrillic as Бакы in Azerbaijani (while the Russian spelling was and still is Баку́ (Bakú)). The modern Azerbaijani spelling, which has been in the Latin alphabet since 1991, is Bakı. The shift from the Perso-Arabic letter و (u) to Cyrillic ы and later Latin ı may be compared to that in other Azerbaijani words (e.g. قاپو (qapu) in old Perso-Arabic spelling with modern Azerbaijani qapı (“door”)), which changed in pronunciation following the development of labial harmony in the Azerbaijani language.
From Bakı + xan + -ov. Originally a title given by the Russian Imperial authorities to the Khans of Baku, similarly to how Şəkixanov and Talışxanov were given to the Khans of Shaki and Talysh.

The lexical component of the calque is probably not transparent to the speakers anymore (if ever?), which is evidenced by the frequent variant azərkeş. Not attested in a dictionary from 1941, but appears in more recent dictionaries. Russian боле́льщик (bolélʹščik) is attested since 1948.
Compare also xəstə (“sick, ill → fan, buff, devotee”), as in futbol xəstəsi 'football fan', meyxana xəstəsi 'meykhana buff'.

etymology notes
Possibly formed as an adjective from aşağa (“downwards”) with the sense "lower, the lower one; low" analogically to yuxarı (“upwards; upper; high”) and later reinterpreted as directional adverb itself. The original form aşağa is now considered colloquial or dialectal and proscribed from usage in writing; as such, it is not found in the standard Azerbaijani dictionaries, such as Azərbaycan dilinin izahlı lüğəti or in Azerbaijani-Russian dictionaries. This is probably due to the fact that the noun *aşaq did not make it into Azerbaijani, so aşağa is not perceived as a dative case of any noun, but rather as a corruption of aşağıya. The latter must be a new dative case form that has been formed with aşağı as the base. Compare also the note on Ottoman Turkish اشغی (aşağı) as a form of Ottoman Turkish اشغه (aşağa) "used by educated people" in Meninski (1680).
The paradigm of directional/spatial adverbs of height in Azerbaijani must have undergone a morpho-semantic leveling so that senses of yuxarı / aşağı and their derived forms almost completely mirror one another:
* yuxarı 'upwards' (adv.); attested first.
** → upper; high (adj); upper part (noun)
*** → new nominal derivations by means of case inflection: yuxarıya (“upwards”), yuxarıdan (“from above”) etc.
* aşağa 'downwards' (adv.); attested first.
** → (analogically with yuxarı) aşağı 'lower'; 'low' (adj);
*** → (analogically with yuxarı) starts being used as a directional adverb 'downwards' along with aşağa and as the noun 'lower part';
**** → new nominal derivations by means of case inflection: aşağıya; aşağıdan etc.
**** → aşağa becomes superfluous in the paradigm, as no equivalent *yuxara exist. It therefore becomes increasingly proscribed.
The formation of aşağı from aşağa as a paradigmatic counterpart of yuxarı may have been facilitated by the need for another, neutral concept for 'low, not high' in view of the development of a negative figurative sense in alçaq (“low; → despicable”).
Compare also reshaping of Turkish aşağı to aşarı, aşaru under the analogical influence of yukarı in Anatolian dialects.

Cognate with Karakhanid [script needed] (boğnaqlān-, “to get cloudy”), Chagatai [script needed] (boğnak, “rainless storm; muffled noise; stifling”), Salar boğunaq (“thunder”), Turkish boğanak (“heavy rain”), boğunuk (“muffled noise”).
From Proto-Turkic *boguŕ (“throat, Adam's apple”). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bog- (“to strangle”). Cognate with Turkish boğaz, Crimean Tatar boğaz, Turkmen bogaz, Chuvash пыр (pyr) etc.
Unclear whether also ultimately from *bog- (“to strangle”).
From Proto-Turkic *bog-. Cognate with Turkish boğmak, Chuvash пӑв (păv).

From boş + -al.
The 2nd sense is a semantic loan from Turkish boşalmak.
Borrowed from Russian бренд (brend), English brand.
From Russian бригада (brigada), from French brigade, Italian brigata.
From Proto-Turkic *bū (“this”) Compare Old Turkic 𐰉𐰆 (b¹w /⁠bu⁠/, “this”).
From Proto-Turkic *būč-gak, from Proto-Turkic *būč- or Proto-Turkic *bïč-. Cognate with Turkish bucak, Chuvash пӗҫмех (pĕśmeh).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish بوداق (budaq), from Proto-Turkic *būtak, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *būta-. Cognate with Turkish budak, Turkmen pudak, Bashkir ботаҡ (butaq), Chuvash пӑта (păt̬a, “nail”), etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic *bulak. Cognate with Turkish bulak, Tatar bolaq, Uzbek buloq.
From Proto-Turkic *bul-. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰉𐰆𐰞 (bul-, “to find, to attain”).
From Proto-Turkic *bulït. Cognate with Turkish bulut, Yakut былыт (bïlït).

glosses: to here, to this place, hither.

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish براقمق (bıraqmaq) Proto-Turkic *bïrak- (“to let; to abandon; to send; to throw”). Cognate with Turkish bırakmak (“to abandon, release, relinquish”), Chuvash пӑрах (părah, “to throw; abandon; stop; let, set”), Gagauz brakmaa.

From buraxıl + -ış.
Virtually all senses developed either as a calque or as a semantic loan from Russian вы́пуск (výpusk), за́пуск (zápusk), до́пуск (dópusk) or про́пуск (própusk).
Internationalism; likely via Russian буржуази́я (buržuazíja), from French bourgeoisie.
From Proto-Turkic *burun. Compare Old Turkic [script needed] (burın, burun).
From bur- + -ğu. Cognate with Turkish burgu (“screw, auger”), Chagatai بورغو (burğu, “screw, drill, auger”), Kazakh бұрғы (burğı, “drill bit, auger”).
Borrowed from Russian буты́лка (butýlka), from Polish butelka, from French bouteille (“bottle”).

From Proto-Common Turkic *bokak, a derivation of Proto-Common Turkic *bok/*buk/*būk (“swelling in the mouth”); alternatively, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *bog- (“to strangle”), whence also Azerbaijani boğmaq and Azerbaijani boğaz. Cognate with Turkish boğak (“tonsillitis, angina”), and dialectal buḫağ (“double chin”).
From Arabic بُخَار (buḵār). Unrelated to Azerbaijani buğ (“steam”).
From Proto-Turkic *bukagu. Cognate with Ottoman Turkish بوقاغی (bukağı).

Izafet II compound of buz + dağ. Calque of English iceberg.

From Proto-Turkic *būg (“steam, fog”). Unrelated to Azerbaijani buxar (“steam”).

From Proto-Turkic *boguday.
Cognate with Turkish buğday, Bashkir бойҙай (buyðay), Kazakh бидай (bıyday), Kyrgyz буудай (buuday), Southern Altai буудай (buuday), Turkmen bugdaý, Uzbek bugʻdoy, Chuvash пӑри (pări, “farro”).
Inherited from Proto-Common Turkic *bȫgček, a derivation Proto-Common Turkic *bȫg.
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (böl-, “to separate”), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bȫl- (“to divide, separate, distinguish”). Cognate with Turkish bölmek, etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic *bedük (“big, high”), whence also Azerbaijani böyütmək (“to raise”) and böyümək (“to grow”). Cognate with Turkish büyük etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic *bedü- (“to grow, increase”). Compare böyük (“big”).
From Proto-Turkic *bürülgen. See Turkish böğürtlen for more.
Equivalent to böyü- + -t. Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Common Turkic *bedü- (“to grow, increase”).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *bȫg. Cognate with Ottoman Turkish بوی (böy), بو (bö), Turkish böğ, bö, Bashkir бөйө (büyü), Kyrgyz бөйү (böyü), бөө (böö).
From French budget, likely via Ottoman Turkish بودجه (büdce) or Persian بودجه (budje).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *bilegü (as reflected in Ottoman Turkish بیلکی (bileği)), from *bi-le- (“to hoon, to sharpen”), from *bī/*bï̄ (“blade”).
From bülöv + -lə. Diachronically, the word contains two suffixes -lə, one of which is no longer recognizable.
From Proto-Turkic *bürü-. Cognate with Turkish bürümek, Chuvash пӗрке (pĕrk̬e).
Borrowed from Russian бюстга́льтер (bjustgálʹter), ultimately from German Büstenhalter.
From Persian بت (“idol”), from Middle Persian bwt' (“Buddha, idol”), ultimately from Sanskrit बुद्ध (buddha).
From Classical Persian بتپرست. By surface analysis, büt + -pərəst
A derivation of *büt- (“to end, accomplish; to create, build; to heal; to grow, ripen”), whence also Azerbaijani bütün (“all”). Cognate with Turkish bitevi.
From Proto-Turkic *bütün, a derivation of *büt- (“to end, accomplish; to create, build; to heal; to grow, ripen”), whence also Azerbaijani bütöv (“whole”).
A derivation of *büt- (“to end, accomplish; to create, build; to heal; to grow, ripen”), whence also Azerbaijani bütün (“all”) and Azerbaijani bütöv (“entire, whole”).

Derivation of Proto-Turkic *bïč- (“to cut”), whence also biçmək (“to cut”).

From Proto-Turkic *bel-le-. Cognate with Turkish bellemek, Chuvash палла (palla).
Borrowed from Arabic بَلْغَم (balḡam), from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma).

From Persian بند. Doublet of banda.

From Persian جیب, from Arabic جَيْب (jayb).

From Persian جفت Doublet of cüt.

Borrowed from Russian чипсы (čipsy), from English chips, plural of chip.

Borrowed from Arabic جِسْمًا (jisman). By surface analysis, cism + -ən.

From cizmək (an old variant of cızmaq) + -gi.
Alternatively, a borrowing from Ottoman Turkish چزگی (whence Turkish çizgi) with the onset voicing due the influence of cızmaq.
Borrowed from Arabic جِزْيَة (jizya), from Middle Persian 𐭢𐭦𐭩𐭲 (gzyt /⁠gazīd⁠/), 𐭢𐭦𐭩𐭲𐭪𐭩 (gzytky /⁠gazīdag⁠/, “poll-tax”).
From Persian جوانمرد (javânmard), from جوان + مرد, whence also Azerbaijani cavan and mərd.
Borrowed from Arabic جُغْرَافِيَا (juḡrāfiyā), from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

Borrowed from Arabic جَوْهَر (jawhar), from Classical Persian گوهر (gawhar). Doublet of gövhər.
Borrowed from Arabic جَوْز (jawz), from Middle Persian 𐭢𐭥𐭦 (gʿz /⁠gōz⁠/).
Borrowed from Turkish cumhurbaşkanı. By surface analysis, cümhur + başqan.

From Persian جفت (joft). Compare Turkish çift.
From Persian جنده. Unclear relationship to cındır.

From Persian جفنگیات (jafangiyyât). By surface analysis, cəfəng + -iyyat

From Arabic جَلْب (jalb). Cognate with Turkish celp.
Borrowed from Classical Persian جَمَادِیُٱلْآخِر (jamādiyu-l-'āxir), from Arabic جُمَادَى ٱلْآخِر (jumādā l-ʔāḵir), ellipsis of شَهْر جُمَادَى ٱلْآخِر (šahr jumādā l-ʔāḵir).

Borrowed from Arabic جَنُوبِيّ (janūbiyy). By surface analysis, cənub + -i.
From Middle Mongol ᠵᠡᠷᠭᠡ (ǰerge), whence also Mongolian зэрэг (zereg).

o.text: Morphologically dağ (“mountain”) + -lıq. The adjectival sense has the adjectival + -lıq suffix.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tāg-. Cognate with Turkish dağılmak.
From Proto-Turkic *tiāĺ, compare Turkish taş, Kyrgyz таш (taş), Chuvash чул (čul).
Borrowed from Russian та́чка (táčka). Influenced by daşımaq.
From Proto-Turkic *taĺ-, *tāĺ-. See cognates at Turkish taşmak.
From daş- (“to overflow”) + -qın. See Bashkir ташҡын (taşqın) for cognates.
From Proto-Common Turkic *taša-. If Chuvash тулт (tult) is a cognate, Proto-Turkic *taĺa- can possibly be reconstructed.
From daşımaq + -n. Cognate with Turkish taşınmak.

Internationalism. Borrowed from Russian дека́брь (dekábrʹ); itself from Old East Slavic декѧбрь (dekębrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic декѧбрь (dekębrĭ), from Medieval Greek Δεκέμβριος (Dekémbrios).
Ultimately from Latin december, from decem + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix.
Internationalism. From Russian демократия (demokratija), ultimately from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā).
Internationalism. By surface analysis, demoqraf(iya) + -ik. Compare Turkish demografik.
From Proto-Turkic *de- (“to say”). Cognate with Turkish demek, Kazakh деу (dew), Chuvash те (te), etc.
Borrowed from Russian депре́ссия (depréssija), from Latin dēpressiō.
Borrowed from Russian дерматология (dermatologija). By surface analysis, dermato- + -logiya.
Internationalism. From Russian девальва́ция (devalʹvácija), itself from German Devalvation, from French dévaluation.
From Proto-Turkic *tebir- (“to capsize, subvert”). Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (devir-), Turkish devirmek, Gagauz devirmää.
From Classical Azerbaijani دِگُلْ (degül), from Old Anatolian Turkish دِكُلْ (degül), from Proto-Turkic *tegül (“is not”). Cognate with Turkish değil, Turkmen däl.
Internationalism; likely via Russian дезинфекция (dezinfekcija), from French désinfection.
From deşmək + -ik, from Proto-Turkic *deĺ- (“to make holes”). Doublet of dəlik. Cognate with Turkish deşik, Turkmen deşik.
Internationalism; ultimately from Ancient Greek διᾰ́λογος (diắlogos, “conversation”).
Borrowed from Russian диа́гноз (diágnoz), from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis).
From dib (“bottom”) + -ək. Compare Ottoman Turkish دیبك, Turkish dibek.

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tï̄t-.
Cognate with Turkish ditmek, Turkmen düýtmek and tüýtmek, Kyrgyz тытуу (tıtuu), Chuvash тат (tat).
Morphologically dik (“steep, upright”) + -si + -in. Cognate with Turkish tiksinmek.
Internationalism. Likely via Russian диктатура (diktatura), from Latin dictatura.

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *til (“tongue; language”). Cognate with Turkish dil.
Further cognates
Cognate with Old Uyghur [script needed] (dïl), Karakhanid [script needed] (dïl), Turkmen dil (“to rise”), Crimean Tatar til, Uzbek til, Uyghur تىل (til) Kazakh тіл (til), Kyrgyz тил (til), Southern Altai тил (til), Tatar тел (tel), Bashkir тел (til), Tuvan дыл (dıl),Yakut тыл (tïl), Chuvash чӗлхе (čĕlh̬e).
Izafet II compound of dil (“language”) + daşıyıcı (“carrier”). Calque of Russian носи́тель языка́ (nosítelʹ jazyká).
Izafet II compound of dil + arxa. Calque of Russian заднеязычный (zadnejazyčnyj).
Borrowed from Russian дилета́нт (diletánt), ultimately from Italian dilettante.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *dil-. Analyzable as *dilmək + -im. See more at dilmek.
Izafet II compound of dil + orta. Calque of Russian среднеязычный (srednejazyčnyj).
Izafet II compound of dil + ön. Calque of Russian переднеязычный (perednejazyčnyj).

Possibly a derivation of Proto-Common Turkic *tint- (“to search”), appended with the suffix -dik (otherwise only found in tapdıq). Alternatively, appended with the suffix -ik. Compare Turkish dimdiklemek.
Derived from Proto-Turkic *dï̄n + -(n)c. Azerbaijani tıncıxmaq (“to pant”) and dincəlmək are derivations of the same root. Cognate with Turkish dinç, Bashkir тыныс (tınıs), see there for more.

From Proto-Turkic *dï̄n, whence also Azerbaijani tıncıxmaq (“to pant”) and dinc (“quite, peaceful”). Morphologically dinc + -əl.
Compare Ottoman Turkish دینجلمك (dincelmek).
From Persian دیندار (dindâr). By surface analysis, din + -dar.
Borrowed from Arabic دِينِيّ (dīniyy). By surface analysis, din + -i.
dinlə- + -mə. Most senses developed either as a calque or as a semantic loan from Russian слушание (slušanije), выслушивание (vyslušivanije) or прослушивание (proslušivanije).

From Proto-Turkic *tïŋla-, *tiŋle- (“to listen”), derived from Proto-Turkic *tiŋ (“reason, mind”). Compare Old Turkic 𐱃𐰃𐰭𐰞𐰀 (tïŋla-, “to listen”). Cognate with Turkish dinlemek, Turkmen diňlemek, Tatar тыңлау (tıñlaw), Kazakh тыңдау (tıŋdaw), Uzbek tinglamoq, Chuvash тӑнла (tănla).
Internationalism. Via Russian диноза́вр (dinozávr), from English dinosaur.

From Proto-Turkic *tīrig.
The sense “undercooked, not overcooked (of rice)“ might have developed from the sense “undercooked (of meat)", the sense “undercooked“ in applying the notion of meat still containing blood, thus being “alive“. Compare Crimean Tatar tiri (“undercooked, of meat”).
From Proto-Common Turkic *tirs-gek, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *tīŕ, whence also Azerbaijani diz (“knee”).
Morphologically, from dirçəl- (“to become animated”, verbal stem) + -iş. Compare diri (“alive”).

Borrowed from Persian دیو (dēw /div).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دیوار (dīvār), from Persian دیوار (divâr).
Internationalism. From Russian дивизия (divizija), from Latin divisio.
Borrowed from Arabic دِيَار (diyār), a plural form of دَار (dār).

Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *tegir- (“to spin, turn”). Compare Azerbaijani dıyır and Azerbaijani dığır all relating to a round object. If Proto-Turkic derivation is true, then doublet of təkər.
From Proto-Turkic *tīŕ, *tǖŕ (“knee”). Cognate with Turkish diz (“knee”).

Izafet II compound of diş (“tooth”) + məcun. The word məcun originally meant "delicious". It developed later the sense "delicious jam or spread" under the influence from the similar sense of semantic loan from Russian па́ста (pásta). The sense "toothpaste" was derived as a semantic parallel semantic loan from or a calque of Russian зубна́я па́ста (zubnája pásta). Alternatively, borrowed from Turkish diş macunu to replace the Russian calque diş pastası.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tōtak (“lip”). Cognate with Turkish dudak, Chuvash тута (tut̬a), Turkmen dōdaq.
From dodaqlan- (“to be pronounced by means of the lips”) + -ma (“negative verbal suffix”) + -yan (“subject non-past participle suffix”). Calque of Russian неогублённые (neogubljónnyje).
Borrowed from Russian дофи́н (dofín), from French dauphin. Doublet of delfin.

glosses: water wheel (a wheel with buckets used to raise water)

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *tolga- (“to twist, to wrap round”). Cognate with Kazakh толғау (tolğaw).
From dolanmaq + -mac. Compare gizlənpaç (“hide and seek”) and atlanbac (“leapfrog”).

Morphologically dolmaq (“to be full”) + -dur.
Cognate with Kazakh толтыру (toltıruw, “to fill”), Turkish doldurmak (“to fill”), Uzbek to'ldirmoq (“to fill”), Kyrgyz толтуруу (tolturuu, “to fill”).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tōl-. Cognate with Turkish dolmak (“to be full”).
From Proto-Turkic *tōlu, from Proto-Turkic *tōl- (“to be full”).

dol + -ça.
From Persian دولچه (dulče), diminutive of دول (dul).
Internationalism; from Russian доме́н (domén), French domaine, ultimately from Latin dominium.
From Proto-Turkic *tōn. Cognate with Chuvash тум (tum).
From Proto-Turkic *toŋ (“frozen; frost”). See Bashkir туң (toñ) for more cognates.

glosses: cloth for sewing a dress, garment

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طوكمق (doŋmaq), from Proto-Turkic *toŋ-.
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (doŋuz, “pig”), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *toŋuz (“pig”).
From Proto-Turkic *tokuŕ (nine). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐱃𐰸𐰆𐰕 (t¹wk¹wz /⁠tokuz⁠/), Turkish dokuz, Chuvash тӑххӑр (tăhhăr), etc.
Morphologically doqquz + -uncu. Cognate with Kazakh тоғызыншы (toğızınšı), Turkish dokuzuncu, Turkmen dokuzynjy.

Borrowed from Classical Persian دوسْت (dōst), from Middle Persian 𐭣𐭥𐭮𐭲𐭩 (dwst' /⁠dōst⁠/), from Old Persian 𐎭𐎢𐏁𐎫𐎠 (d-u-š-t-a /⁠dauštā⁠⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *jawštā́, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́awštā́, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéws-tōr ~ *ǵus-tr-és, from *ǵews-.
From Proto-Turkic *tabɨĺgan (“hare”). Cognate with Turkish tavşan.
From Proto-Turkic *tokuŕ ōn, equivalent to doqquz (“nine”) + on (“ten”).
From Proto-Turkic *tog-. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (tugur-, “to give birth to”), Uzbek tugʻmoq (“to give birth to”), Chuvash ту (tu).
From doğramaq (“to cut into small pieces, chop, crumble”) + -mac. Compare the semantic parallel to окро́шка (okróška).

Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *dogra- (“to cut into slices, small pieces”).
Cognates
Cognate with Karakhanid [script needed] (toɣrāmāk, “to cut into slices”), Crimean Tatar doğramaq (“to cut into slices”), Turkish doğramak (“to chop, hack”), Bashkir турау (toraw, “to cut, chop, hack, kill”), Chuvash турама (turama, “to crumble, chop up”), Kazakh турау (tuwraw, “to cut, slice, crumble”), Khakas тоғырирға (toğırirğa, “to cut, chop, crumble”), Kyrgyz тууроо (tuuroo, “to cut into slices”), Turkmen dogramak (“to cut into pieces”), Tuvan доораар (dooraar, “to cut into pieces”), Uyghur توغرىماق (toghrimaq, “to cut up, chop”), Uzbek toʻgʻramoq (“to cut, mince”).

Likely a semi-learned borrowing from Late Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (*toğu) that was only attested in compounds in the Ottoman translations of Quran into Old Anatolian Turkish since 1424. Otherwise, directly borrowed from Turkish doğu. Likely used since 1960s or 1980.
From Russian дрон (dron), from English drone.
Borrowed from Russian дубля́ж (dubljáž), from French doublage.
From Proto-Common Turkic *tuman, a derivative of the verbal stem Proto-Common Turkic *tuma-, *tum- (“to envelop”).
From duman (“fog”) + -lıq. The sense “nebula” is a semantic loan from Russian тума́нность (tumánnostʹ).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طورمق (durmaq), from Proto-Turkic *tur- (“to stand”) Cognate with Turkish durmak, Turkmen durmak, Crimean Tatar turmaq, Uzbek turmoq, Uyghur تۇرماق (turmaq), Kazakh тұру (turuw), Tatar turu, Chuvash тӑр (tăr).
From Proto-Turkic *turńa. Cognate with Turkish turna, Chuvash тӑрна (tărna), etc.
From dur- (“to stand”) + -um. The senses 'situation' and 'condition' are a semantic loan from Turkish durum.

From earlier dutsaq, from Old Anatolian Turkish طوتساق (dutsaq), from Old Anatolian Turkish طوتمق (dutmaq). By surface analysis, tut- (“to catch, capture, arrest”) + saq. Cognate with Turkish tutsak (<Ottoman Turkish طوتساق).
From Persian دستاقخانه (dostâqxâne). By surface analysis, dustaq (“prisoner”) + -xana.
From Proto-Turkic *tuy- (“to perceive (by ears or nose), notice”). Cognate with Turkish duymak.
From duy- (“to feel; to become aware of”) + -uq.
From duy- (“to feel”) + -ğu. Cognate with Turkish duygu.
Borrowed from Turkish duygulanmak. Equivalent to duyğu + -lan.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طُوزْ (duz), from Proto-Turkic *tūŕ.

From Proto-Common Turkic *tuzak (“snare, trap”).
Cognate with
Old Uyghur [script needed] (tuzaq, “snare, trap”);
Turkish tuzak,
Kazakh тұзақ (tuzaq),
Kyrgyz тузак (tuzak),
Southern Altai тузак (tuzak),
Uzbek tuzoq,
Bashkir тоҙаҡ (tuðaq),
Tuvan дузак (duzak),
Yakut туһах (tuhaq, “snare, trap”),
etc.
From Proto-Turkic *töle-, Old Anatolian Turkish دوللك (“place where sheep breed”).
From Proto-Turkic *tȫn-. Cognate with Karakhanid [script needed] (tȫnmēk, “to return”), Turkish dönmek.
From dön- (“to turn”) + -əm. The sense 'period' is a semantic loan from Turkish dönem.
Borrowed from Turkish döner, from Turkish döner kebap, from dönmek + kebap. Cognate with Azerbaijani dönmək (“to (re)turn”).
From Turkish dönerci or equivalent to dönər + -çi.
From dörd + -üncü. Cognate with Kazakh төртінші (törtinši), Turkmen dördünji, Turkish dördüncü.
Borrowed from Persian دُوران, from Arabic دَوَرَان (dawarān).
Borrowed from Arabic دَوْرِيّ (dawriyy). By surface analysis, dövr + -i
From Proto-Turkic *tȫg- (“to pound”). Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (tög-, “to pound, crush”), Turkish dövmek.
From döy- (“to beat, to beat up”) + -üş. Cognate with Turkish dövüş.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دویمك (döymek), دوزمك (dözmek), from Proto-Turkic *töŕ-, whence also Hungarian tűr (“to endure, tolerate”).
From Proto-Common Turkic *töše-. By surface analysis, döş + -ə.
From Proto-Common Turkic *tüŋür (“relative by marriage”). Cognate with Turkish dünür.
Ultimately calque of English worldview. Izafet II compound of dünya + görüş.

From Arabic دُنْيَوِيّ (dunyawiyy). By surface analysis, dünya (“world”) + -vi.
The shift from the sense mundane to secular is probably resulting from a semantic loan from Russian светский (svetskij).
Cognate with Uzbek dunyoviy.

From Proto-Turkic *tün (“night, yesterday”)
Cognate with
Old Turkic 𐱅‬𐰇‬𐰤 (tün, “night, dark night”),
Turkish dün (“yesterday”),
Turkmen düýn (“yesterday”),
Crimean Tatar tünevin (“yesterday”) and dün (“yesterday”),
Karachay-Balkar тюнене (tünene, “yesterday”),
Uzbek tun (“night”),
Uyghur تۈن (tün, “dark”) and تۈنۈگۈن (tünügün, “yesterday”),
Tatar төн (tön, “night”),
Bashkir төн (tün, “night”),
Kazakh түн (tün, “night”) and
Kyrgyz түн (tün, “night”).

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (döğü). In Ottoman Turkish less commonly دوكی (düğü, “rice”). Compare Turkish düğü (“the finest bulgur than remains after sifting”). Cognate with Kumyk дюгю (dügü, “rice”), Salar dügü, Turkmen tüwi (“rice”), Chagatai توکی (twky /⁠tügi⁠/, “rice”), Uyghur تۈگە (tüge, “millet”). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *düg- (“to pound”), whence also Azerbaijani döymək (“to beat, to beat up, to knock”). The term referred to various pounded cereals, later gaining the sense "pounded rice" and, finally, "rice" in general.
Morphologically düymək + -ün. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (tügün).
Calque of Russian прямоуго́льный треуго́льник (prjamougólʹnyj treugólʹnik).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دوزمك (düzmek), from Proto-Turkic *tüŕ-. Cognate with Turkish and Turkmen düzmek, Gagauz düzmää.
From Old Anatolian Turkish دوش (düş, “dream, vision”), from Proto-Turkic *tǖĺ (“dream”).

From düşün- + -cə.
Cognate with
Turkish düşünce.
Uzbek tushuncha,
Bashkir төшөнсә (tüşünsä).

From Proto-Turkic *til (“tongue”). The change from front to back vowel predates the earliest written record in the 11th century. Cognate with Turkish dılak, Kazakh тылақ (tılaq). Compare also Kyrgyz тилчик (tilcik).
A derivation from Proto-Turkic *dïrŋa- (“to scratch, scrape”). Cognate with Bashkir тырма (tırma), see it for more cognates.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دیرنق (dırnaq), from Proto-Turkic *tïrŋak. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐱃𐰃𐰺𐰭𐰴 (tïrŋaq, “fingernail”), Turkish and Crimean Tatar tırnak, etc.
Izafet II compound of dırnaq (“quotation mark”) + ara (“the space between”). Perhaps a calque of Russian в кавы́чках (v kavýčkax).
Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *tegir- (“to spin, turn”). Compare Azerbaijani diyir and Azerbaijani dığır all relating to a round object.
From Armenian տղա (tġa), ultimately from Classical Syriac ܛܠܝܐ (ṭalyāʼ, “boy”).

glosses: thread or a wool on a spool

o.text: Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *tegir- (“to spin, turn”). Compare dialectal dığarax (“spool”). Also compare Azerbaijani diyir and Azerbaijani dıyır all relating to a round object.

Inherited from Ajami Turkic [script needed] (dışxarı) (likely influenced by Chagatai [script needed] (tašqarı)), from Old Anatolian Turkish دشره (daşra) (attested in "Destân-ı Yûsuf" in the 13th century), from Proto-Common Turkic *tašgaru.
Cognate with Turkish dışarı, Gagauz dışar, Chuvash тол (tol).

From Middle Mongol [Term?]; whence also modern Mongolian дуулга (duulga), from Proto-Mongolic *dugulga. Possibly via Chagatai دبولغه (dubulğa), توبولغا (tubulğa) (→ Uzbek dubulgʻa), unless the fortition of /-v~w-/ to /-b-/ was an independent development in Azerbaijani.
Compare also Old Anatolian Turkish توغلقه (toğulga, tuğulga), Ottoman Turkish توولغه, تولغه, تولقه, تغلغه, توغلغه, Kazakh дулыға (duwlığa), Kyrgyz туулга (tuulga), Southern Altai туулга (tuulga), Kumyk давулгъа (dawulğa).
The Mongolic terms is likely a Turkic borrowing itself, compare Karakhanid تُوغْلُغْ (tuğluğ), Old Turkic [script needed] (tuğluğ, tuğlığ), a derivation from Old Turkic [script needed] (tuğ, “tug, horse tail hairs”).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دفنی (defni), from Greek δάφνη (dáfni).
Borrowed from Arabic دَفْتَر (daftar), ultimately from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra).
From Persian دفترخانه. By surface analysis, dəftər + -xana.
From dəhşət (“horror”) + -izm. The function of the suffix is unclear.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دلو (delü), from Proto-Turkic *tēlbe (“mad, stupid”). Cognate with Turkish deli, Uzbek telba, Turkmen däli and telbe, Southern Altai тели (teli), Tatar тилбә (tilbä, “foolish person”), Chuvash тилӗр (tilĕr, “become enraged”) etc.
By surface analysis, dəl- + -ik, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *teĺ-. Doublet of deşik. Cognate with Turkish delik.
Borrowed from Persian دَلَّاک, from Arabic دَلَّاك (dallāk).

glosses: tear (a drop of clear, salty liquid produced from the eyes by crying or irritation)

o.text: Possibly from Proto-Turkic *tam- (“to burn; to kindle; to become excited”). Cognate with Kyrgyz там- (tam-, “to catch fire”), тамызуу (tamızuu, “to catch fire”). Alternatively, same as Etymology 2.
From Proto-Turkic *temür. Doublet of Teymur (given name).
Izafet II compound of dəmiryol + keçid. Calque of Russian железнодорожный переезд (železnodorožnyj perejezd).
From Proto-Turkic *temregü (“a skin condition”), a derivation from *temür (“iron”). Cognate with Turkish temriye.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دَكِزْ (däŋiz), from Proto-Turkic *teŋiŕ, whence also Hungarian tenger (“sea”). Cognate with Turkish deniz, Tatar диңгез (diñgez), Bashkir диңгеҙ (deñgið), Kazakh теңіз (teŋiz), Uyghur دېڭىز (dë'ngiz) Chuvash тинӗс (tinĕs, “sea”), etc.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دَكَمَكْ (däŋämäk, “to compare, measure; to try”), from Proto-Turkic *teŋe- (“to value, compare”), a derivation from Proto-Turkic *teŋ (“equal”). Cognate with Turkish denemek.
Borrowed from Turkish dergi, where it was reintroduced as a learned borrowing from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (dẹrgü, “tablecloth, napery”).

From Proto-Turkic *tẹri (“skin”). Cognate with Turkmen deri, Turkish deri,
Kazakh терi (teri),
Karachay-Balkar тери (teri), Kumyk тери (teri), Kyrgyz тери (teri),
Uzbek teri,
Uyghur تېرە (tëre),
Yakut тирии (tirii), Dolgan тирии, Tatar тире (tire) and
Bashkir тире (teri).
From Proto-Turkic *teriŋ (“deep”). Cognate with Turkish derin, Bashkir тәрән (tärän), Chuvash тарӑн (tarăn) etc.
Morphologically, from dərin (“deep”) + düşüncə (“thought, thinking”) + -li. Probably a calque of Russian глубокомы́сленный (glubokomýslennyj).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish درمان (dermān), from Persian درمان (darmân).
From Proto-Common Turkic *tēr-. Cognate with Turkish dermek.

Likely from Late Ottoman Turkish درنك (dernek), a learned borrowing from a medieval Turkic language, such as Karakhanid تِرْناكْ (tẹrnek, “people's gathering, a public assembly”), from earlier *tẹringek, from *tērin-, a passive/reflexive form of Proto-Common Turkic *tēr- (“to gather, collect”). From Proto-Turkic *kẹlin (“bride, daughter-in-law”). Probably a derivation from Proto-Turkic *kẹl- (“to come”), whence also Azerbaijani gəlmək. The etymology is probably based on the fact that a daughter-in-law used to be a newcomer in her husband's extended household. Starostin et al. reject the seemingly obvious relation between the two roots in favor of the form *kele reconstructed for the largely discredited Proto-Altaic. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰚𐰠𐰤 (kelin /⁠kl²n²⁠/, “daughter-in-law”), Turkish gelin (“daughter-in-law”), Gagauz gelin (“bride”), Bashkir килен (kelin, “bride, young wife”), etc.

The term being overrepresented makes it difficult to pinpoint the original source. For a similar case, see alış-veriş, alqı-satqı.

According to Nişanyan, from Persian پای (pây, “foot”), with the sense ”share” originating from the Persian expression borrowed into Old Anatolian Turkish بای برابر (pây-berâber, “equally, to the same proportion”, literally “equal foot”). The word is present in its modern sense in XIVth century Book of Dede Korkut.
The non-Oghuz Turkic cognates, such as Kirgiz and Yakut пай (pay, “share”) are, according to Nişanyan, a borrowing from the Ottoman Turkish پای, via Russian пай (paj).
However it is more possibly borrowed from Middle Chinese 派 (pʰaiH) as early as 7th century and inherited by later Turkic languages.

From pay + -la.

Borrowed from Russian пе́нис (pénis), from Latin pēnis (“tail, penis”).
Borrowed from Russian пе́нсия (pénsija), ultimately from Latin pensio.

From perspektiv + -siz.
Calque of Russian бесперспекти́вный (besperspektívnyj).
From Persian پیمانکار. By surface analysis, peyman + -kar.

From Classical Persian پِلَّه (pilla), whence also Azerbaijani pilləkən via the plural form in Persian. Compare Georgian ფილა (pila).
From Classical Persian پلکان, plural of پله (pilla, “step of a staircase”), whence the Azerbaijani pillə. Compare Armenian փիլաքյան (pʻilakʻyan) and Georgian ფილაქანი (pilakani).

From pilotsuz (“pilotless”) + izafet II compound of uçuş (“flight”) + aparat (“device”).
Calque of Russian беспило́тный лета́тельный аппара́т (bespilótnyj letátelʹnyj apparát).

Probably from Armenian փնթի (pʻntʻi, “slovenly, untidy”) or Persian پنتی (penti), پینتی (pinti).
Compare also Mamluk Kipchak [script needed] (pinti, “wretched, helpless”), and Ottoman Turkish پنتی (penti, pinti, “stingy”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (pišik), from Proto-Common Turkic *pišik.
Internationalism; ultimately from Latin planēta and Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”).
From Persian پلاو (pelâv), via Russian плов (plov).

From Russian политкорре́ктный (politkorréktnyj) + -lik, partial calque of Russian политкорре́ктность (politkorréktnostʹ), from an abbreviation of Russian полити́ческая корре́ктность (politíčeskaja korréktnostʹ), ultimately from English political correctness.
Borrowed from Russian помидо́р (pomidór), from Italian pomi d'oro.
Borrowing from Russian по́нчик (pónčik), from Polish pączek.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پورتقال (portakal, “orange”), which, in non-standard dialects, also was pronounced with غ (ğ).
From Proto-Turkic *botu (“young of camel”). Cognate with Tatar and Bashkir бута (bota), Kyrgyz бото (boto), Kazakh бота (bota).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish پوخ (poḫ), from Proto-Turkic *bok (“dirt, dung”). Cognate with Turkish bok, Salar boq, Chuvash пӑх (păh) etc.

From pox + -lu.
Cognate with Turkish boklu

From Proto-Turkic *buŕ-, *boŕ- (“to damage, destroy”).
Cognate with Turkish bozmak, Chuvash пӑс (păs, “break, destroy”), etc.
Borrowed from Russian почта (počta), from Polish poczta, from Italian posta.
Ultimately from Italian postiglione, via French postillon, via Russian почтальо́н (počtalʹón).
Internationalism; likely via Russian преамбула (preambula), from French préambule, ultimately from Medieval Latin praeambulum.
Borrowed from Russian премьера (premʹjera), itself derived from French première.
Borrowed from Russian прести́ж (prestíž), from French prestige.
Internationalism; via Russian президент (prezident), from French président, from Latin praesidens.
Internationalism; ultimately from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma).
Internationalism; ultimately from Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”).
Internationalism; likely via Russian пролета́рий (proletárij), ultimately from Latin prōlētārius.
Borrowed from Russian пролетариа́т (proletariát), from French prolétariat.
Borrowed from Russian проло́г (prológ), ultimately from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).
From proqram (“program”) + təminatı (“provisions”). Calque of Russian програ́ммное обеспече́ние (prográmmnoje obespečénije).
Borrowed from Russian проспе́кт (prospékt), from German Prospekt, from Latin prospectus (“view, sight”).
Borrowed from Russian протеже́ (protežé), from French protégé.
Borrowed from Russian провока́ция (provokácija), ultimately from Late Latin provocatio.
Ultimately from French psychologie, reinterpreted as an adjective.
Borrowed from Russian психометрия (psixometrija). By surface analysis, psixo- + -metriya.
From Persian پررنگ (porrang), from پر (por, “full”) + رنگ (rang, “colour”). Equivalent to Azerbaijani pür + rəng.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *püskür- (“to spurt, splutter”). Onomatopoeic in the older root form püf or püs. By surface analysis, püs (“blowing and spurting sound”) + -kür. Compare Turkish püskürmek.
From Persian پسته, doublet of fıstıq (“beech”).
Borrowed from Persian پستهای (peste-'i). By surface analysis, püstə + -i.
Calque of Persian پناه بردن (panâh bordan, literally “carry refuge”).
Calque of Persian پناه آوردن (panâh âvardan, literally “bring refuge”).
Izafet II compound of pəncərə + alt. Calque of Russian подоко́нник (podokónnik)
From Persian پرچین. Cognate with Turkish perçin.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kāp (“bowl, cup”); cognate with Karakhanid قابْ (qāp), Turkish kap, Turkmen gap (“box, bag”), Tatar кап (qap, “box, bag, case”).

From Mongolic, ultimately from Middle Mongol 合班.
Cognate with Tuvan хаван (xavan), Kazakh қабан (qaban), Kyrgyz каман (kaman), Northern Altai кабан (kaban), Southern Altai каман (kaman), Nogai кабан (kaban), Tatar кабан (qaban), Kumyk къабан (qaban), Karachay-Balkar къабан (qaban), Turkish kaban (dialectal), Uzbek qobon, etc.

glosses: eve, threshold (the time preceding some event)

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *k(i)amak, *k(i)apak (“forehead; front; part; eyelid; eyebrow”). Cognate with Turkish kabak, Uzbek qovoq (“eyelid”), Khakas хамах (xamax, “forehead”), Bashkir ҡабаҡ (qabaq, “eyelid”) etc.

From Proto-Turkic *kāpuk (“bark; skin; shell”).
Analyzable as qab + ıq.
From Proto-Turkic *KApur. Cognate with Turkmen gapyrga, Crimean Tatar qaburğa, Bashkir ҡабырға (qabırğa).

Possibly from Proto-Turkic *kad-, whence also Azerbaijani qayğı; however, the intervocalic /d/ instead of expected /j/ is not quite clear.
Alternatively, from Proto-Common Turkic *kada- (“to thrust into, to plunge into”).
Compare dialectal Turkish gada.

glosses: a metal patch used to repair cracks

o.text: From qada- (“to thrust into, to plunge into”) + -q.

From Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠ (qadaɣa), ᠬᠠᠳᠠᠭᠠᠯᠠ (qadaɣala), itself a borrowing from Turkic, compare Old Turkic [script needed] (qadaɣla, “to guard, protect”), a derivation of Old Turkic [script needed] (qadaɣ). Possibly ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *kād-, whence also Azerbaijani qayğı (“care”).
Cognate with Turkish kadağa. Compare Persian قدغن, Georgian ყადაღა (q̇adaɣa), Northern Kurdish qedexe, Turkic borrowings.

Inherited from Proto-Common Turkic *xātun (“queen, lady”). The form in the standard language was likely reintroduced by intellectuals influenced by the Ottoman language around 1900 after a few centuries of disuse (see the quotation from 1914).

From Classical Azerbaijani [script needed] (qafa), from Old Anatolian Turkish قفا (qafa), from Arabic قَفًا (qafan, “back of the head; nape of the neck”).
Cognate with Turkish and Gagauz kafa.
From Arabic غَافِل (ḡāfil). Doublet of qəfil.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kāla- (“to pile up, to stack”). The fire-related sense developed from the sense "to heap up firewood".
Morphologically from qalxmaq (“to rise”) + -dır, with /x/ in qalxmaq being lost via syncope. Cognate with Turkish kaldırmak.

From Proto-Turkic *kiāl-mak (“to stay behind, remain”).
Cognates
Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰴𐰞 (qal-, “to be left (behind)”), Old Uyghur [script needed] (qal-, “to remain”), Karakhanid قَلْماقْ (qalmāq, “to remain”), Turkish kalmak (“to remain, stay”), Bashkir ҡалыу (qalıw, “to remain”), Chagatai [script needed] (qalmaq, “to remain”), Chuvash юлма (julma, “to remain”), Kazakh қалу (qaluw, “to remain”), Khakas халарға (xalarğa, “to remain”), Kipchak [Arabic needed] (qal-, “to remain, stay”), Kyrgyz калуу (kaluu, “to remain”), Tatar калу (qalu, “to remain”), Turkmen gālmak (“to remain”), Tuvan калыр (kalır, “to remain, stay”), Uyghur قالماق (qalmaq, “to remain”), Uzbek qolmoq (“to remain, stay”), Yakut хаал (qaal, “to remain, stay”).
From Persian قالمقال (qâl-maqâl), from Arabic قَال وَمَقَال (qāl wamaqāl).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kalpak. See more at English calpack and Turkish kalpak.
Borrowed from Russian га́лстук (gálstuk), ultimately from German Halstuch (“neckerchief”) or Dutch halsdoek (“neckerchief”).
Borrowed from Russian голубо́й (golubój), whence also the semantic loan mavi (“light blue; homosexual”).
From qalxana (“shield”) (dative) + bənzər (“similar”). Likely a calque of Russian щитови́дный (ščitovídnyj).

From Proto-Turkic *kalï- (“to rise”)
Cognates
Cognate with Old Uyghur [script needed] (kalı-, “to rise in the air”), Karakhanid [script needed] (kalɨ̄māk, “to buck, jump”), Turkish kalkmak (“to rise, ascend, get up”), Bashkir ҡалҡыу (qalqıw, “to rise”), Kazakh қалқу (qalquw, “to soar”), Kyrgyz калкуу (kalkuu, “to float”), Southern Altai калыыр (kalïïr, “to jump, hop”), Tatar калку (qalqu, “to rise”), Turkmen galkmak (“to rise”), Tuvan халыыр (xalıır, “to jump, run”), Uzbek qalqmoq (“to rise, swell, jump”), Yakut кылый (kïlïy, “to hop along”).
From Proto-Turkic *kalïŋ (“thick; numerous”). Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (kalïn, “thick”), Turkish kalın.
Borrowed from Russian га́мбургер (gámburger), from English hamburger.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kamčï (“whip”), a derivation from *kam- (“to beat, strike down”).
From Proto-Turkic *kamïĺ. Cognate with Chuvash хӑмӑл (hămăl, “stubble; stalk of cereals”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish قان (qan), from Proto-Turkic *kān (“blood”).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *kānat. Cognate with Turkish kanat, Kazakh қанат (qanat), etc.

Provided the etymology proposed by Vasmer is correct: from Russian кандалы́ (kandalý), ultimately from Arabic قَيْدَان (qaydān), dual form of Arabic قَيْد (qayd, “fetter, chain, bond”); thus, a doublet of qeyd (“registration”). Ukrainian кайдани (kajdany) and Polish kajdany preserve the original /j/.
Perhaps from Proto-Turkic *kān- (“to be satisfied”). Probably cognate with Turkish kanmak (“to believe; to be satisfied”), Turkmen ganmak (“to satisfy one's thirst; to study, master”).
Borrowed from Arabic قَانُون (qānūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn).
Univerbation of qanuna + uyğun. Calque of Russian закономе́рный (zakonomérnyj).
From Arabic قَانُونِيّ (qānūniyy). By surface analysis, qanun + -i.
Izafet III compound of qanun + alilik. Calque of Russian верхове́нство зако́на (verxovénstvo zakóna).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kap-gak, ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *kap-. Cognate with Turkish kapak.
From Proto-Turkic *kap-. Cognate with Turkish kapmak, Chuvash хып (hyp), etc.
From Old Anatolian Turkish قاپو (qapu). Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *kap- (“to close, cover”). Cognate with Turkish kapı.
Morphologically qapı (“door”) + -çı. Cognate with Crimean Tatar qapıcı.
Morphologically from qapmaq (“to snatch”) + -ış. From Proto-Turkic *kap- (“to snatch”). Cognate with Turkish kapışmak.
From Proto-Turkic *kār (“snow”). Cognate with Turkish kar, Chuvash йор (jor).
From Proto-Turkic *kara. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (kara, “black”), Turkish kara, Chuvash хура (hura), etc.
Borrowed from Russian гара́ж (garáž), from French garage.
From qarala + -ma. Cognate with Turkish karalama.

From qara (“black”) + -şın, which is otherwise only attested in sarışın and in the borrowed name Aqşın.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قرداش, قردآش (qardaš). Equivalent to qarın (“womb”) + -daş (“fellow, sharer”). Literally, “those who share the same womb”. Compare Turkish kardeş.

glosses: foreshank, shoulder; upper part of the front leg of a sheep

o.text: From Proto-Common Turkic *karmak (“fishing rod; hook”). See Bashkir ҡармаҡ (qarmaq) for more cognates.
From Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠷᠠᠭᠤᠯ (qaraɣul). Cognate with Turkish karakol, Uzbek qorovul, Persian قراول (qarâvol).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kārt- (“falcon, hawk”). Cognate with Turkish kartal.
From Proto-Turkic *karga (“crow”). See Bashkir ҡарға (qarğa) for more cognates.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قرغامق (qarġamaq), from Proto-Turkic *karga-. Compare Turkish kargımak, Crimean Tatar qarğamaq.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قارغیش (qarġış), قَارِشْ (qarış), from Proto-Common Turkic *kargïš, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *karga-. By surface analysis, qarğı- + -ş. Compare Turkish kargış.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قرن (qarın), from Proto-Turkic *karïn. Cognate with Turkish karın.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kiarïnč-ɣa, from Proto-Turkic *karïnčga (“ant”). Doublet of qarışqa. Cognate with Turkish karınca, Crimean Tatar qarınca, Turkmen garynja (“ant”).
From Proto-Turkic *kār- (“to mix”) Cognate with Turkish karmak.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kiarïnč-ɣa, from Proto-Turkic *karïnčga (“ant”). Doublet of qarınca. Cognate with Turkish karınca, Crimean Tatar qarınca, Turkmen garynja (“ant”).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *kar-. Cognate with Turkish karşı.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kasïrku. Cognate with Turkish kasırga. Compare Chuvash косӑрка (kos̬ărk̬a, “blizzard”), possibly a Kipchak borrowing.

glosses: a kind of bandolier sewn into a military uniform or into a traditional festival dress

o.text: From Persian قطار (qatâr), from Arabic قِطَار (qiṭār, “train”).
From Proto-Turkic *kat-. Cognate with Turkish katmak, etc.
From Proto-Turkic *kat. Cognate with Chuvash хытӑ (hyt̬ă), etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kaya, from Proto-Turkic *k(i)aya. See more at Turkish kaya.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kayïna-, a derivation of Proto-Common Turkic *kań, *kïń.
Calque of Russian горя́чая ли́ния (gorjáčaja línija), ultimately from English hotline.

A derivation of Proto-Turkic *kay- (“to turn back”), whence also Azerbaijani qayıtmaq (“to come back”). Cognate with Karakhanid قَیْتَرْماق (qaytarmāq, “turn back”), which Kashgari reported to be an Oghuz word, Kipchak qaytar- (“to return something”).
Ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *kaïčï; compare Mongolian хайч (xaič), Bashkir ҡайсы (qaysı).
From Classical Persian خایه گینه (xâya gina, “a kind of scrambled eggs”).
From Proto-Turkic *kadgu (“sorrow”). Cognate with Turkish kaygı, Uzbek qaygʻu, Chuvash хуйхӑ (hujh̬ă, “grief, sorrow”), Bashkir ҡайғы (qayğı) (see more there).
By surface analysis, qayıt- (“to come back”) + -ış.

glosses: brother-in-law, specifically, the brother of one's spouse

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *kādïn (“relative-in-law”), whence also qayınana (“mother-in-law”) and qayınata (“father-in-law”). Compare Turkish kayın (“in law”), Tatar каенага (qayınağa, “older brother of one's wife”), and каенэне (qäyenene, “younger brother of one's wife”).

From Proto-Common Turkic *kadïr- (“to bend, turn, twist”).
Unrelated to Turkish kayırmak (“to favor, to protect”), which is cognate with Turkish kaygı, Azerbaijani qayğı etc. instead (from Proto-Turkic *kadgu).

Possibly from Proto-Turkic *kay- (“to turn back; to show respect; to squint; to move to smb.'s side; to run towards; to go past, around”). Cognate with Karakhanid قَدِتْماقْ (qadïtmāq, “to come back”), Turkish kayıtmak, Crimean Tatar qaytmaq, Bashkir ҡайтыу (qaytıw).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kadï-. See cognates at Bashkir ҡайыш (qayış).

glosses: sucker, mark, someone who is easy to swindle or con

o.text: Borrowed from Russian каземат (kazemat), ultimately from Italian casamatta.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *kaŕgan, compare Chuvash хуран (huran).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قزانج (qazanç). By surface analysis, qazan- + -c. Cognate with Turkish and Gagauz kazanç.
From Proto-Turkic *kaŕgan- (“to earn”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰴𐰕𐰍𐰣 (qazɣan-, “to conquer, gain, win”), Turkish kazanmak, Chuvash хӑрхӑн (hărh̬ăn, “miser”).
From qazanılmış (“acquired”) + immun çatışmazlığı (“immune deficiency”) + sindrom (“syndrome”). Calque from English.
From Proto-Turkic *kaŕ-. Cognate with Turkish kazmak, Chuvash хыр (hyr).
Morphologically qazmaq (“to dig”) + -ıntı. Probably a calque of Russian ископаемое (iskopajemoje).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kač- (“to run away, flee”). Cognate with Turkish kaçmak etc.
From qaç- (“to run”) + -ır. Compare Turkish kaçırmak.

From Proto-Common Turkic *kāš (“eyebrow; edge”), possibly from Proto-Turkic *kāĺ (“eyebrow; edge”). Cognate with Turkish kaş, etc.
The sense 'gemstone' might have developed from in the following way: 'eyebrow' → 'curved object' → 'ring frame' → 'gemstone', although it has sometimes also been seen as unrelated to the sense 'eyebrow'.
From Proto-Turkic *kaĺčï- (whence also qaşımaq (“to scratch”)). Cognate with Turkish kaşağı.
From Proto-Common Turkic *kaška-lak, from Proto-Common Turkic *kaška (“bald/white spot on the forehead”), thus equivalent to qaşqa + -laq.
From Old Anatolian Turkish قاشق (qašuq, qašıq), from Proto-Turkic *kaĺuk (“spoon”). Compare Turkish kaşık.
Likely borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قائب ایتمك. Compare Turkish kaybetmek, from the Arabic-derived kayıp + Turkish etmek, and its Gagauz cognate kaybetmää.
Borrowed from Arabic قَيْد (qayd). Doublet of qandal.
The accumulation of the senses mark, note, and celebrate in one item is probably a result of the semantic loan from Russian отметить (otmetitʹ).

From Proto-Turkic *kïyn (“hard, difficult”).
Cognate with Kumyk qıyın, Kazakh қиын (qıyın, “difficult”), Kyrgyz кыйын (kıyın, “difficult”), Uzbek qiyin (“difficult”).
Borrowed from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr). Cognate with Turkish gayr (Ottoman Turkish غیر (gayr)), Turkmen gaýr, Uyghur غەير (gheyr), Uzbek gʻayr.
From the third-person singular possessive form of qeyr (“another”), from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr). Compare Turkish gayri (Ottoman Turkish غیری (gayri)), Turkmen gaýry, Uzbek gʻayri.
Borrowed from Arabic غَيْرِيّ (ḡayriyy). By surface analysis, qeyr + -i. Cognate with Turkish gayri (Ottoman Turkish غیری (gayrî)), Turkmen gaýry, Uyghur غەيرىي (gheyriy), Uzbek gʻayri.
Borrowed from Classical Persian غیرـ (ġayr-i-), from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr) + Persian ezafe. Cognate with Turkish gayri- (Ottoman Turkish غیر (gayr-i)), Uyghur غەيرى (gheyri), Uzbek gʻayri-.
From Arabic غَيْر طَبِيعِيّ (ḡayr ṭabīʕiyy). From qeyri- + təbii.

Calque of Russian нетрадиционной ориентации (netradicionnoj orijentacii, “of non-traditional [sexual] orientation”).
By surface analysis, qeyri-ənənəvi orientasiya + -lı.
From Arabic غِذَاء (ḡiḏāʔ). Compare Turkish gıda.
From Classical Persian قرائت (qirā'at), from Arabic قِرَاءَة (qirāʔa).
Borrowed from Arabic قِسْمًا (qisman), adverbial accusative of قِسْم (qism). By surface analysis, qisim + -ən.
From Arabic قِيَاسِيّ (qiyāsiyy). By surface analysis, qiyas + -i
From Russian гобой (goboj), from French hautbois.
Analysable as qoca + -man. Compare Turkish kocaman.
From Arabic قوم (qawm, “tribe, family”). Doublet of qövm.

glosses: branch (stream which flows into a larger river)
goal (act of placing the object into the goal)

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *kol (“upper arm”). Cognate with Turkish kol, Crimean Tatar qol etc.
From qol (“arm; hand”) + -ay. Compare Turkish kolay.
From qolay + -lan. Perhaps from the dialectal sense of qolay 'direction, way, side'.

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (qonuq). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kon- (“spend the night”), whence also Azerbaijani qonşu (“neighbour”). Compare Turkish konuk (“guest”), Crimean Tatar qonaq (“meeting room”), Chuvash хӑна (hăna, “guest”).
Izafet II compound of qonaq (“guest”) + otaq (“room”). Calque of Russian гости́ная (gostínaja).

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (qonuq). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kon- (“spend the night”), whence also Azerbaijani qonşu (“neighbour”) and Azerbaijani qonaq (“guest”). Compare Turkish konuk (“guest”), Crimean Tatar qonaq (“meeting room”), Chuvash хӑна (hăna, “guest”).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish قُنكشٖی (qoñşı), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kon- (“neighbour; friend; guest”), whence also Azerbaijani qonaq (“guest”). Compare Turkish komşu, Uzbek qoʻshni, Turkmen goňşy, Kyrgyz кошуна (koşuna, “guest”), Kumyk хоншу (xonşu).
From Proto-Turkic *kȫŕ/kōŕ, back vowel variant of Proto-Turkic *kȫŕ, whence the doublet köz (“ember”).
From Proto-Common Turkic *kōrï-. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (korï-, “to protect”), Uzbek qoʻrimoq (“to protect”).
Morphologically qoruq (“protected place, reserve”) + -çu. Cognate with Ottoman Turkish قوریجی (korucu, korıcı), Uzbek qoʻriqchi.
Morphologically from qorxmaq + -aq. Cognate with Turkish korkak, Uzbek qo'rqoq, Kyrgyz коркок (korkok), Kazakh қорқақ (qorqaq) Bashkir ҡурҡаҡ (qorqaq), Tatar куркак (qurqaq), Uyghur قورقاق (qorqaq).
From Proto-Turkic *kork-. Cognates include Turkish korkmak, Kazakh қорқу (qorquw), Uzbek qoʻrqmoq, Chuvash хӑра (hăra).
Morphologically from qorx- + -u. Cognate with Turkish korku.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *kotuz. Cognate with Turkish kotaz, dialectal Tatar кутаз (qutaz).

Perhaps also influenced by the form qurd (“worm”), as the finger movement resembles a moving worm while poking/picking at something.

Borrowed from Persian سرحد (sarhad), from Persian سر (sar) + Arabic حَدّ (ḥadd).
Borrowed from Persian سرلوحه. By surface analysis, sər + lövhə.
Borrowed from Classical Persian سَرْتِیب (sartīb), an archaic variant of سَرْتِیپ (sartīp, “brigadier”).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *serče. Cognate with Turkish serçe, Chuvash ҫерҫи (śerś̬i).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *ses. Cognate with Turkmen, Crimean Tatar, Gagauz, Turkish ses, Kazakh сес (ses), Chuvash сасӑ (sas̬ă).
Partial calque of Turkish ses kasmak

Calque of Russian голосова́ть (golosovátʹ). Literally, “to give voice”.
Compare Turkmen ses bermek, Uzbek ovoz bermoq, Kazakh дауыс беру (dawıs berüw), and Kyrgyz добуш берүү (dobuş berüü), all with the same meaning from the same source.
Izafet II compound of səs (“voice, sound”) + yazı (“text, writing”). Calque of Russian звукозапись (zvukozapisʹ).
Borrowed from Arabic سطحي. By surface analysis, səth + -i.
Borrowed from Classical Persian سَیَاحَت (sayāhat), from Arabic سِيَاحَة (siyāḥa).

glosses: all the way (adds emphasis to the measurement of a physical or temporal distance; coupled with kimi (“until”), qədər (“until”), -dək (“until”) or -cən (“until”))

o.text: Calque of Persian تاب آوردن (literally “to bring endurance”).
Borrowed from Persian تباشیر, from Hindi तबाशीर (tabāśīr), from Sanskrit तवक्षीर (tavakṣīra)
From Arabic تَاج (tāj), ultimately of Iranian origin.
Borrowed from Turkish takipçi. Doublet of təqibçi (“pursuer, chaser, follower; crake”).
Internationalism; via Russian та́ктика (táktika), ultimately from Ancient Greek τακτικός (taktikós, “fit for ordering”).
Of Mongolic origin. Ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *tala, *tal-b- (“steppe, open place”), whence also Modern Mongolian тала (tala).
From tala + -n. Cognate with Ottoman Turkish تالان (talan), Chagatai [script needed] (talay, talan).
Calque of Russian соверше́нно секре́тный (soveršénno sekrétnyj, literally “completely secret”).
Borrowed from Arabic تَمَامًا (tamāman), adverbial accusative of تَمَام (tamām). By surface analysis, tamam + -ən.
From tam + dəyərli. Likely a calque of Russian полноце́нный (polnocénnyj).
Internationalism. From English tank, from Portuguese tanque, from Gujarati ટાંકી (ṭā̃kī).

Old Anatolian Turkish تكری (teŋri)
Azerbaijani tanrı
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish تكری (teŋri), from Proto-Turkic *teŋri.

Etymology tree
Proto-Turkic *teŋri
Old Anatolian Turkish تكری (teŋri)
Azerbaijani tanrı
Proto-Turkic *-či
Azerbaijani -çi
Azerbaijani tanrıçı
From tanrı (“god”) + -çı (“-ist”).

From Proto-Turkic *tanu- (“to know, get to know”) Cognate to Turkish tanımak, Turkmen tanamak, Kazakh тану (tanuw), Kyrgyz тануу (tanuu), Salar danı, Uyghur تونۇماق (tonumaq), Chuvash тынӑ (tynă, “eyewitness”).

Most likely reborrowed from Persian تپانچه (tapânča), from Ottoman Turkish طبانجه (tabanca, “palm of the hand; slap; trigger of a gun; handgun”), derived from طبان (taban, “sole”), corresponding to Azerbaijani daban (“heel”).
From tapda- + -ala. Possibly a derivation of Proto-Turkic *tep-, *dēp- (“to stamp, tramp”) and related to Azerbaijani təpik (“kick”). Probably ultimately of onomatopoetic origin.
From tap- + -maca, an unproductive suffix that is perhaps only present in boğmaca and çəkməcə.

From Proto-Turkic *tap- (“to find”). Not cognate with Turkish tapmak (“to worship”), which is derived from a different root (akin to Azerbaijani tapınmaq (“to worship”)).
Cognates
Cognate with dialectal Turkish tapmak (“to find”), Crimean Tatar tapmaq, Turkmen tapmak, Uzbek topmoq, Uyghur تاپماق (tapmaq), Chuvash туп (tup).

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (tapšurmaq). Cognate with Turkish tapşırmak, Uzbek topshirmoq (“to deliver, hand over, present”), Uyghur تاپشۇرماق (tapshurmaq), Kyrgyz тапшыр (tapşır, “to hand over; to assign”).
From tapşır- + -ıq. Cognate with Uyghur تاپشۇرۇق (tapshuruq).

Borrowed from Russian тарака́н (tarakán), possibly a Turkic borrowing itself. Inheritance from an ancestor Turkic language would rather have yielded Azerbaijani *taraqan/*daraqan (or *tarağan/*darağan).
Borrowed from Arabic تَارِيخِيّ (tārīḵiyy). By surface analysis, tarix + -i.
Borrowed from Arabic تَارِيخًا (tārīḵan), adverbial accusative of تَارِيخ (tārīḵ). By surface analysis, tarix (“history”) + -ən.

From Proto-Common Turkic *tar + -la. This noun-deriving suffix is also present in Azerbaijani çağala, yayla and damla. Cognate with Turkish tarla and Chagatai تارلا (tarla, “sown field”).
Compare a similar formation with the same base of derivation and the suffix -lag in Chagatai [script needed] (tarlag), Cuman-Kipchak tarlov, Kumyk тарлав (tarlaw), Nogai тарлав (tarlav), Karachay-Balkar тарлау (tarlau), Bashkir and Tatar тарлау (tarlaw), Khakas тарлағ (tarlağ, “ploughed field”).
Alternatively, from Old Anatolian Turkish *tarï-la, from Proto-Oghuz *tarïg-lag, supposed cognate of Karakhanid تَرِغْلاغْ (tarïğlāğ), Old Uyghur 𐾀𐽰𐽾𐽶𐽲𐾁𐽰𐽲 (tʾryqlʾq /⁠tarïġlaġ⁠/) and
Old Turkic 𐱃𐰺𐰍𐰞𐰍 (t¹r¹g¹l¹g¹ /⁠tarïɣlaɣ⁠/),
going back to Proto-Common Turkic *tarïg-lag.

glosses: basin (a wide bowl for washing, sometimes affixed to a wall)
match (a series of games, played until one player reaches three points, for example by winning three single games (oyuns), or a single game and a gammon (mars).)

o.text: From Arabic طَاس (ṭās), ultimately from Middle Persian tšt'. Doublet of teşt.
From Persian طاس (tâs), from Middle Persian tʾs (tās, “die, dice”).
From Turkic, from Proto-Common Turkic *tasma (“leash, strap”). Cognate with Kumyk тасма (tasma), Bashkir таҫма (taśma).
From Proto-Turkic *tak- (“to bind to, add to”). Cognate with Turkish takmak, etc.
From Persian تخته بندی (taxtebandi). Equivalent to taxta + bənd.

From Old Anatolian Turkish تخيل (taxïl), from Arabic دَخْل (daḵl).
Doublet of dəxl.

glosses: sack (usually used for grains or potatoes)
counter for bags of grain or potato
one side of something; especially bank (of a river etc.)

o.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 對 (twojᴴ). Akin to Persian تای (tāy), Russian тай (taj), and the first part of Georgian თაიგული (taiguli).
From tay + -keş. Cognate with dialectal Turkish taykeş.

glosses: procumbent (trailing) stem of plants like watermelon, melon, cucumber

o.text: Ultimately from Classical Persian تغار. Doublet of dağar.
Internationalism; via Russian теа́тр (teátr), from French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron).

From Proto-Turkic *tēl (“wire, string; thong; strand”). Cognate with Karakhanid تِلیٖ (tili, “thong”), Crimean Tatar and Turkish tel, Turkmen til, Kumyk and Nogai тел (tel), Chuvash тал (tal, “bundle”).
Alternatively, related to Armenian թել (tʻel, “thread”), either as a direct borrowing or originating from the same Iranian source.
The sense 'telegram' is possibly a phono-semantic matching of Azerbaijani teleqram.
Internationalism; from French téléphone, from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “afar”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”).
From Russian телеканал (telekanal). By surface analysis, tele- (“tele-”) + kanal (“channel”).
Blend of telekanal (“TV channel”) + kanalizasiya (“sewerage, drainage; canalization”). Also can be analyzed as tele- (“tele-”) + kanalizasiya. Compare Russian телеканализация (telekanalizacija).
Internationalism; via Russian телегра́ф (telegráf), ultimately from French télégraphe.
Borrowed from Russian терапе́вт (terapévt), from Ancient Greek θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs).
Borrowed from Russian термо́метр (termómetr), ultimately from French thermomètre.

Internationalism; Russian те́хника (téxnika), from German Technik, from Latin technica, from Ancient Greek τεχνική (tekhnikḗ).
The military sense is a shortening of hərbi texnika.
Internationalism; via Russian техноло́гия (texnológija), from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología, “systematic treatment (of grammar)”).
Ultimately from French technologie, reinterpreted as an adjective.

Reborrowed from Classical Persian تیز (tēz), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *teŕ-, doublet of Azerbaijani təzmək. Cognate with Crimean Tatar tez, Kazakh тез (tez), Tatar тиз (tiz), Uzbek tez, Chuvash тар (tar, “to run away”).
Izafet II compound of tibb (“medicine”) + bacı (“sister”). Calque of Russian медсестра́ (medsestrá).
Borrowed from Arabic طِبِّيّ (ṭibbiyy). By surface analysis, tibb (“medicine”) + -i.
From Proto-Common Turkic *tiken, equivalent to tikən, present participle of tikmək (“to sew”). Also, Compare to Southern Altai тегенек (tegenek), тиген (tigen, “fir”).

From Proto-Turkic *tik- (“vertical; to plant vertically”).
Compare Turkish dikmek (“to sew”), Kumyk тикмек (tikmek, “to sew; to build”) Kazakh тігу (tigüw).
From Proto-Common Turkic *tikö (“piece”). Compare Turkish tike (“piece”), Turkmen tike, Kyrgyz тике (tike), биртике (birtike, “a little bit”), Khalaj tike, Karakhanid تِكُو (tikǖ, “piece, slice”).

glosses: edge (the joining line between two vertices of a polygon)
ridge or top (of an elongated hill)

o.text: From Arabic طِلَسْم (ṭilasm), from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “payment”).
Borrowed from Arabic تِمْسَاح (timsāḥ), from Coptic ⲙⲥⲁϩ (msah), from Egyptian G17-O34:V28-I3 mzḥ (“crocodile”).
Internationalism; via Russian тип (tip), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos).
Likely a calque of Russian тиражи́ровать (tiražírovatʹ). By surface analysis, tiraj + -la.
From Russian тире (tire), ultimately from French tiret.
Borrowed from Persian تریاک, from Ancient Greek θηριακή (thēriakḗ).
Ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *top (“all, completely”) + -la. Cognate with Turkish toplamak.

glosses: set (a (mostly abstract) object made up of several parts)
collection (a set of items or amount of material procured or gathered together)
totality (an aggregate quantity obtained by addition)

o.text: From Proto-Common Turkic *top-ïk. By surface analysis, top (“round thing; ball”) + -uq.
Etymologically from toxu- + -uş. Ultimately derived from Proto-Turkic *tokï- (“to weave”). Cognate with Turkish tokuşmak.
Inherited from Proto-Common Turkic *tor. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (tor, “net”), Southern Altai тор (tor, “net”).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طوپراق (ṭopraq), from Proto-Turkic *toprak (“earth, soil”). Developed through metathesis, compare Turkish toprak. Cognate with Azerbaijani toz.
Cognates
Cognate with Crimean Tatar topraq, Bashkir тупраҡ (topraq), Kazakh топырақ (topıraq), Kyrgyz топурак (topurak), Kyrgyz тобрак (tobrak), Tatar туфрак (tufraq), Turkmen toprak, Tuvan довурак (dovurak), Uzbek tuproq, Uyghur تۇپراق (tupraq), dialectal Yakut тобурах (toburaq, “dust”), Chuvash тӑпра (tăpra).

Ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *tod- (“become satiated, full”) and a doublet of doyğun, therefore equivalent to *tos- + -qun. The first syllable coda /-s/ points towards borrowing of a reflex with a /-ð/, with subsequent devoicing.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tokïmak (“club, mallet”), a derivation from *tokï- (“to hit, strike”).
The sense “tangent” is a calque of Russian касательная (kasatelʹnaja).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طوی (toy), from Proto-Turkic *toy (“feast”). Compare Turkish toy, Gagauz toy.

From Proto-Turkic *tiakïgu (“hen, fowl”).
Cognate with
Turkish tavuk,
Uzbek tovuq,
Kazakh тауық (tawıq),
Kyrgyz тоок (took),
Bashkir тауыҡ (tawıq),
Tatar тавык (tawıq),
Old Uyghur 𐾀𐽰𐽲𐾄𐽶𐽲𐽳 (takïgu)
etc.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طُوزْ (doz), from Proto-Common Turkic *tōz.
Per Bəşirov, comes from earlier *toza- + -anaq. Alternatively, it may be derived from Proto-Turkic *tōzan (“dust”) + -aq.

Present participle compound of toz (“dust”) + sormaq (“to suck”).
Calque of Russian пылесос (pylesos). Attested since at least 1966.
From English tramway or from French tramway.
From English trolley bus, ultimately via Russian тролле́йбус (trolléjbus).
From Proto-Common Turkic *tūč. Cognate with Turkish tunç.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tōr- (“young of an animal”). See more at Turkish torun.
From Persian توت (tut). Ultimate origin uncertain.
From reduplication of tut- (“to catch, to arrest”).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish طوتمق (dutmaq), from Proto-Turkic *tut-. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐱃𐰆𐱃 (tut-, “to keep, catch, own”), Turkish tutmak (“to catch, keep”), Bashkir тотоу (tutuw, “to keep, hold”), Chuvash тытма (tytma, “to keep, hold”), Khakas & Shor тударға (tudarğa, “to keep, hold, catch, seize, rule, hold back”), Kyrgyz тутуу (tutuu, “to catch”), Turkmen tutmak (“to hold, keep, catch, hire, fill”), Tuvan тудар (tudar, “to hold, catch, grab”), Uzbek tutmoq (“to take, hold, catch”), Yakut тут (tut, “to hold, seize, grab, catch”).
From tutu (“parrot”, from Classical Persian طُوطِی (tūtī)) + quşu (definite accusative of quş (“bird”))
Borrowed from Mongolic, from Proto-Mongolic *tokoi (“elbow, river bend”). See more at Kazakh тоғай (toğay).

glosses: flourish (a ceremonious passage such as a fanfare)
dream (imaginary events seen in the mind while sleeping)

o.text: Borrowed from Russian туш (tuš), from German Tusch, probably from French touche.
Borrowed from Russian тушь (tušʹ), from German Tusche, from French touche, from toucher (“to touch”).
From Proto-Turkic *tök-. Cognate with Turkish dökmek, see there for more cognates.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دوریمك (dörẹmek), دورومك (dörümek) Proto-Turkic *törü- (“to be born, originate”), ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *töŕ. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (törü-, “to come into being, to be generated”), Turkish türemek, Gagauz türümää, Turkmen döremek.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دوریدمك (döredmäk). Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (törüt-, “to bring into being, to generate”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (tüfeng), from which also Ottoman Turkish تفنك (tüfenk) and Persian تفنگ (tofang). Cognate with Karakhanid [script needed] (tüwek), Nogai туьбек (tübek).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish توك (tüg, tük), from Proto-Turkic *tǖk.
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (düken-), reflexive of Proto-Common Turkic *tüke- (“to come to an end”). See more at Turkish tükenmek.
From Proto-Turkic *tülki, *tilkü (“fox”). Cognate with Turkish tilki, Bashkir төлкө (tülkü) etc.
Borrowed from Russian тюльпа́н (tjulʹpán), from obsolete French tulipan, from New Latin tulipa, from Italian tulipano, from Turkish tülbent (“turban”), from Persian دلبند (dolband, “turban”).
From tülə- (“to moult”) + -k. Cognate with Kazakh түләк (tüläk).

glosses: toman (a Persian money of account or gold coin issued until 1927)

o.text: Borrowed from Persian تومان (tumân), ultimately same as above.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ترك (türk), from Proto-Turkic *tür(ü)k.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish تركی (türkī), By surface analysis, türk + -i.
Borrowed from Persian ترکمان (torkamân). Doublet of türkmən.
Probably from Russian тюрьма́ (tjurʹmá), although the Russian word most probably has a Turkic source. See Bashkir төрмә (türmä) for more.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *tütsüg. Cognate with Turkish tütsü.
Ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *tüt(e)- (“smoke, to smoke”), whence also Azerbaijani tüstü (“smoke”).

From Proto-Turkic *tï̄n, whence also Azerbaijani dincəlmək (“to rest”) and dinc (“quite, peaceful”). Cognate with Bashkir тынсыу (tınsıw), Tatar тынчу (tınçu), Kazakh тыншу (tınšuw, “stuffy, poorly ventilated”), Kumyk тунчукъ (tunçuq, “stuffy, poorly ventilated”).

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (taš-baqa), equivalent to daş (“stone”) + bağa (“turtle; earlier: frog”).
Cognates
Cognate with Turkish tosbağa, Chagatai [script needed] (taš-baqa),Uzbek toshbaqa, Bashkir ташбаҡа (taşbaqa), Kazakh тасбақа (tasbaqa), Tatar, Kyrgyz ташбака (taşbaka), Uzbek toshbaqa, Uyghur تاشپاقا (tashpaqa, “turtle, tortoise”).
Analyzable as tıxa- + -c. Cognate with Turkish tıkaç. Compare Turkmen dyky. The senses 'congestion' and 'traffic jam' are a semantic loan from Russian про́бка (próbka).
From Proto-Turkic *tɨkɨ- (“to stuff in, press in”). Cognate with Turkish tıkamak and Azerbaijani tıxmaq (“to devour, to gobble”)
From Arabic تَبَدُّلَات (tabaddulāt), plural of تَبَدُّل (tabaddul).
From Arabic تَبَعَة (tabaʕa), plural of تَابِع (tābiʕ).

Arabic تَجَاوُز (tajāwuz)bor.
Azerbaijani təcavüz
Borrowed from Arabic تَجَاوُز (tajāwuz), from تَجَاوَزَ (tajāwaza).
Borrowed from Classical Persian تَجَاوُزْکَار (tajāwuzkār). By surface analysis, təcavüz + -kar.
From Arabic تَجْهِيزَات (tajhīzāt). By surface analysis, təchiz + -at.
From təcrid (“isolation”) + -xana. Possibly a calque of Russian изоля́тор (izoljátor).

From Arabic تَدْقِيقَات (tadqīqāt), plural of تَدْقِيق (tadqīq). By surface analysis, tədqiq + -at.
Compare Turkish tetkikat.
Borrowed from Arabic تَفْصِيلًا (tafṣīlan), adverbial accusative of تَفْصِيل (tafṣīl). By surface analysis, təfsil + -ən.
From təhlükəsiz + -lik. Calque of Russian безопа́сность (bezopásnostʹ).
Izafet II compound of təhlükəsizlik (“safety”) + kəməri (“belt”). Ultimately calque of English safety belt, likely via Russian реме́нь безопа́сности (reménʹ bezopásnosti).
From Arabic تَحْقِيقَات (taḥqīqāt). By surface analysis, təhqiq + -at.
From Persian تحقیرآمیز. By surface analysis, təhqir + -amiz.
Borrowed from Arabic تَحْرِيف (taḥrīf), verbal noun of حَرَّفَ (ḥarrafa, “to distort, to corrupt, to falsify, to misconstrue, to pervert, to twist”).
From Arabic تَحْرِيم (taḥrīm). The South Azerbaijani senses are copied from Persian تحریم (tahrim).

From Arabic تَحْصِيل (taḥṣīl).
Compare Turkish tahsil.
From Proto-Turkic *tēk. Cognate with Turkish tek, Turkmen täk, Tatar and Bashkir тик (tek), Kazakh тек (tek), Tuvan тик (tik, “zero”) etc.
Borrowed from Arabic تَأْكِيدًا (taʔkīdan), adverbial accusative of تَأْكِيد (taʔkīd). By surface analysis, təkid + -ən.

Arabic تَكْلِيف (taklīf)bor.
Azerbaijani təklif
Borrowed from Arabic تَكْلِيف (taklīf), from كَلَّفَ (kallafa).
From Latin repetitio est mater studiorum (“repetition is the mother of knowledge”).
From təktanrıçı + -lıq. Cognate with Turkish tek tanrıcılık.
From Proto-Turkic *teke/*tekä/*täkä. Cognate with Chuvash така (tak̬a, “male animal”).
From Proto-Turkic *teker. Cognate with Old Turkic tegrek (“ring, circle”), and the root *tegir- (“to spin, turn”). Related to dəyirman. See Turkish teker and Bashkir тәгәрмәс (tägärmäs) for more.
Borrowed from Arabic تَلَاطُم (talāṭum), verbal noun of تَلَاطَمَ (talāṭama, “to clash, to brawl”).
From Persian تلاش, itself borrowed from a Turkic source.
Ultimately from Arabic طَلَبَات (ṭalabāt), plural of طَلَب (ṭalab).
Borrowed from Arabic طَلَبَة (ṭalaba), plural of طَالِب (ṭālib, “seeker, pursuer; student, scholar”).
Derived from Arabic تَمْيِيز (tamyīz). Doublet of təmyiz.
Borrowed from Persian تمبر (tambr), from French timbre (“stamp”).
Borrowed from Arabic تَمْيِيز (tamyīz). Doublet of təmiz.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تمل, ultimately from Ancient Greek θεμέλῐος (themélĭos).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دَكْ (däŋ), from Proto-Turkic *teŋ (“equal”).
Present participle compound of tən (“equal”) + böl- (“to divide”).
Borrowed from Classical Persian تَنْقِید (tanqīd), a pseudo-Arabism from the root ن ق د (n q d).
From tənqidi (“critical”) + təfəkkür (“cognition, thinking”). Ultimately a calque of English critical thinking via Russian крити́ческое мышле́ние (kritíčeskoje myšlénije).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دپوك (depük). By surface analysis, təp- + -ik.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دپمك (depmek), from Proto-Turkic *tep- (“to stamp, tramp”).
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 疊子 (dep tsi^X, “small dish; plate”), via Middle Mongol. Cognate with Turkish tepsi, Karakhanid تَڤْسٖی (tewsi) and Old Uyghur 𐾀𐽶𐽼𐽻𐽶 (typsy /⁠tépse⁠/). Doublet of tepşi.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دَپَه (däpä), تَپَه (täpä), from Proto-Turkic *tepe.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish دپه كوز (däpä göz). By surface analysis, təpə + göz.
From Arabic تَقْدِيمَات (taqdīmāt). By surface analysis, təqdim + -at.
Borrowed from Arabic تَقْرِيبًا (taqrīban), adverbial accusative of تَقْرِيب (taqrīb). By surface analysis, təqrib + -ən.
From Proto-Turkic *tẹr. Cognate with Karakhanid تَرْ (ter), Turkish ter, Chuvash тар (tar), etc.

From tərbiyə + -çi.
Calque of Russian воспита́тель (vospitátelʹ).
Borrowed from Persian ترجمه حال (tarjome-ye hâl).
From Proto-Turkic *depre- (“to move, stir, shake”) + -n. Cognate with Turkish deprenmek.
From Persian ترسا (tarsâ). Doublet of tərs.
Borrowed from Classical Persian طرفدار (tarafdār). By surface analysis, tərəf + -dar.
First element borrowed from Persian تره (tara /tare). Compare the Persian compound ترهبار (tara-bār /tare-bâr, “vegtables”).
Borrowed from Arabic تَصَادُفًا (taṣādufan). By surface analysis, təsadüf + -ən.
From təsir (“influence”) + -çi. The social media sense is a calque of English influencer.
From Classical Persian تأسیس (ta'sīs), from Arabic تَأْسِيس (taʔsīs).
From Arabic تَصْنِيفات (taṣnīfāt), from Arabic تَصْنِيف (taṣnīf).
Borrowed from Arabic تَصْوِير (taṣwīr), from صَوَّرَ (ṣawwara).

Most likely borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تتك (tetik), reflecting the historical spread of firearms from Ottoman Turkey to Safavid Iran. Ultimately derived from Proto-Turkic *tet-, thus related to didmək.
Borrowed from Arabic تَخْمِينًا (taḵmīnan), adverbial accusative of تَخْمِين (taḵmīn). By surface analysis, təxmin + -ən.
From Arabic تَأْيِينَات (taʔyīnāt). The sense "purpose, function" is likely a semantic loan from Russian назначе́ние (naznačénije).
From Arabic تَعْيِينِيّ (taʕyīniyy), nisba of تَعْيِين (taʕyīn).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طیاره (tayyare), itself derived from the Arabic ط ي ر (ṭ y r, “related to flying”). Attested no earlier than 1910s.
Ultimately from Arabic ض م ن (ḍ m n, root); compare Ottoman Turkish تضمینات (tazmînât), Turkish tazminat (“compensation”).
Ultimately from Arabic تَضْيِيق (taḍyīq). Cognate with Turkish tazyik, Uzbek tazyiq.
From Proto-Common Turkic *tezek, from Proto-Turkic *teŕ-. Cognate with Chuvash тирӗс (tirĕs), etc.
From Arabic تَشْكِيلَات (taškīlāt). By surface analysis, təşkil + -at
Calque of Persian تشریف بردن (literally “bring honor”).
Calque of Persian تشریف آوردن (literally “bring honor”).
From təşviq + -at. Senses influenced by Russian агита́ция (agitácija).
From Arabic تَشَكُّل (tašakkul), verbal noun of تَشَكَّلَ (tašakkala, “to become shaped, formed”).
From Arabic تَأَثُرَات (taʔaṯurāt), plural of تَأَثُّر (taʔaṯṯur).

According to Dybo, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *yüg-, hence Azerbaijani yüksək and other related forms. Compare Turkish yüce and dialectal yüvcek, yüğcek, üğücek.
According to Sevortyan, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ūč (“edge”), hence, related to Azerbaijani uc (“tip, point, cusp”) and unrelated to Azerbaijani yüksək.
Some consider both the Turkish uca (“coccyx”) and Azerbaijani uca (“high”) to be derived from Proto-Common Turkic *ūča. The semantic developments that led to the emergence of both these senses could have been along the lines of 1) 'edge' -> 'top of a tree' -> 'high'; 2) 'edge' -> 'edge of the body' -> 'rump; back; loins, buttocks'. Sevortyan, however, considers these two forms unrelated.
Compare Kipchak یوجا (yuca); Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (yüce); Old Turkic [script needed] (uča, “coccyx”).
None of the forms above are thought to be related to uçmaq (“to fly”), despite a certain semantic link.

From Proto-Common Turkic *ūčuz, cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (učuz, “easy”), Karakhanid اُجُزْ (učuz, “worthless”), Turkish ucuz, Turkmen ujyz, Tatar очсыз (oçsız), Bashkir осһоҙ (ushuð, “cheap”), Southern Altai очы (očï, “small”), etc.
From ud- (“to swallow”) + -laq or udul- (“to be swallowed”) + -aq.
From Proto-Turkic *yubut- (“to swallow”). Cognate with Turkish yutmak, Chuvash ҫӑт (śăt), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *ut- (“to win”). Cognate with Turkish utmak.
From ud- + -uz. Cognate with dialectal Turkish yutuzmak.

graft (small shoot or scion of a tree inserted in another tree)

glosses: to joint, connect, to attach, to stitch on

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یلدوز (yulduz), from Proto-Turkic *yulduŕ.

Izafet II compound of ulduzlar + ara. Likely a calque of Russian межзвёздный (mežzvjózdnyj). Cognate with Turkish yıldızlararası, Turkmen ýyldyzlarara, Uzbek yulduzlararo, Kazakh жұлдызаралық (juldızaralıq), Kyrgyz жылдыздар аралык (jıldızdar aralık).
Borrowed from Turkish uluslararası. By surface analysis, izafet II compound of uluslar + ara. First attested in 2021.
Borrowed from Russian унита́з (unitáz), from Latin ūnitās (“unity”).
Borrowed from Russian университе́т (universitét), from German Universität, from Latin universitas.
From Proto-Turkic *umnït-. Cognate with Chuvash ман (man, “to forget”). See Turkish unutmak for more.
From Proto-Common Turkic *ur. Cognate with Turkish ur, etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic *ubut (“shame”) + -an. Cognate with Turkish utanmak.
Borrowed from Russian увертю́ра (uvertjúra), from French ouverture.
