o.text: From Proto-Turkic *ud- (“to follow, conform”). Compare Turkish uymak.

glosses: to match, to tally, to correspond, to agree
to join, to reach, to reunite (with)

o.text: From the syncope of Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (uyuχu) (?); ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ūdï-.
From Old Anatolian Turkish اوزاق (uzaq), from Proto-Turkic *uŕak (“long, far, late”), whence also uzun (“long, tall”).

Present participle compound of uzaq (“far”) + vurmaq (“to strike”).
Calque of Russian дальнобо́йный (dalʹnobójnyj).
Ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *ūz + -laş, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *ūŕ.
From Proto-Turkic *uŕïn, whence also uzaq (“far, distant”).
From uzun (“long, tall”) + dıraz, the second part from Persian دراز (derâz, “long”).

glosses: to fly (to travel through the air)

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish اوچمق (uçmaq), from Proto-Turkic *uč- (“to fly”).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish اوچماق (uçmaq), واچماغ (uçmağ), from Proto-Turkic *uštmag, from Sogdian [script needed] (ʼwštmʼχ, “paradise”). Sogdian borrowing underwent a semantic merge with uçmaq (“to fly”), thence the parallels.
Cognate with Kazakh ұжмақ (ujmaq), Southern Altai учмак (učmak), etc. Doublet of behişt.
Derivation from Proto-Turkic *uč- (“rash, inflammation, pustules on lips; catarrh, cold, fever; to appear (of rash), catch cold”).
Calque of Russian взлётно-поса́дочная полоса́ (vzljótno-posádočnaja polosá).
From earlier *uğuramaq, ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *ugur, whence also Azerbaijani uğur.
Onomatopoeic. Equivalent to uğ (“buzzing sound”) + -ulda (verb forming suffix).
From Proto-Common Turkic *ugur (“to meet; to intend; occasion, reason, time”).

From Proto-Common Turkic *uša- (“small”), alternatively reconstructed as *uvša-.
Cognate with Turkish uşah (“child”) (dialectal, Zonguldak, Bartın, Karabük, the Black Sea Region, Kırşehir), uşak (“male child”) (dialectal, Ordu), and Gagauz uşak (“child”).

Izafet II compound of uşaq (“child”) + bağça (“garden”).
Calque of Russian детский сад (detskij sad).
From Persian واهمه, from Arabic وَهِمَ (wahima).
Internationalism; via Russian вакцина (vakcina) or French vaccin.

Borrowed from Arabic وَالِدَيْن (wālidayn), oblique dual of وَالِد (wālid, “father, parent”). The Arabic form already means “parents”, but was additionally suffixed with the Azerbaijani plural ending, and the singular meaning “parent” was then backformed. Related with övlad (“child”), which is from the same Arabic root (and also a backformed singular).
Borrowed from Russian валю́та (valjúta), Italian valuta (“currency”), from Latin valeō (“to be worth”).
Borrowed from Russian вампи́р (vampír), from French vampire or German Vampir, from Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь.
Borrowed from Russian ваго́н (vagón), from French wagon, from English waggon, from Middle Dutch wagen.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish وار (var), from Proto-Turkic *bār. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰉𐰺 (bar).
From Proto-Turkic *bar- (“to walk, go; to come, reach”). Cognate with Turkish varmak, Uzbek bormoq, Chuvash пыр (pyr), etc.
From Russian вайфа́й (vajfáj), from English Wi-Fi.
Partial calque of Persian باز آمدن (bâz âmadan). Cognate with Turkish vazgeçmek.
From Russian вокзал (vokzal), ultimately from English Vauxhall.
From Arabic وَجْه (wajh). Doublet of vəch.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish وِیرْكُو (vergü), from Proto-Turkic *bērgi. By surface analysis, ver- (“to give”) + -gi.
From veril- (“to be given”) + -iş. The sense 'program' is a calque of Russian переда́ча (peredáča).
Literally, “those that are given”. Calque of Russian да́нные (dánnyje), ultimately a calque of Latin data.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ویرمك (vẹrmek), from Proto-Turkic *bēr- (“to give”). Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (ber-, “to give”), Turkish vermek, etc. For the sense 3, compare Turkish vermek and Russian дать (datʹ).
From Russian винт (vint, “screw”), from Polish gwint, from German Gewinde.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ویران (vīrān) Persian ویران (virân). Doublet of örən.
Borrowed from Russian витри́на (vitrína), French vitrine (“shop window, display case”).
Borrowed from Russian ви́це-президе́нт (více-prezidént). By surface analysis, vitse- + prezident.
From Russian вор в законе (vor v zakone).
Sense 2 (“multiplication”) is a calque of Arabic ضَرْب (ḍarb).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish اورمق (urmaq), from Proto-Turkic *ur-. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰆𐰺 (ur-), Turkish vurmak, Uzbek urmak, etc.
The sense to multiply is a semantic loan from Arabic ضَرَبَ (ḍaraba, “to multiply”).
Likely from Turkish vurgulamak. By surface analysis, vurğu + -la.
Onomatopoeic. Equivalent to vız (“buzzing sound”) + -ılda (verb forming suffix).
From Arabic وَ (wa). Cognate with Turkish ve, Turkmen we
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish وافتیس or from Turkish vaftiz. Ultimately from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ولی (velī), from Classical Persian ولی (walē).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ولی (velī), from Arabic وَلِيّ (waliyy).
Borrowed from Arabic وَلَد الزِّنَى (walad az-zinā).
From Persian ورزش. Doublet of vərziş.
From Persian ورزش. Doublet of vərdiş.
From Arabic وَسَائِط (wasāʔiṭ). The sense 'handbook' is a semantic loan from Russian посо́бие (posóbije).
From Classical Persian وَصِیَّتنَامَه (wasiyyat-nāma). By surface analysis, vəsiyyət + -namə.

Calque of Russian гражда́нский бра́к (graždánskij brák), literally "civil marriage".
Note that the definition below does not include the English sense civil marriage.

Equivalent to vətən + -pərvər, from Arabic وَطَن (waṭan, “homeland”) and Persian پرور (parvar), from پروردن (parvardan). Compare Ottoman Turkish وطن پرور (vatanparver), where the word appears for the first time in 1860s.
From Persian وطنپرست (vatan-parast); equivalent to vətən (“homeland”) + -pərəst.
From Proto-Turkic *bẹńŕ (“swelling; scar, ulcer”) cognate with Turkish bez, пӳр (pür, “pus”), etc.

Borrowed from Arabic وَزْنَة (wazna, “particular weight”). Compare also Persian وزنة (vazna, vaznat, “weight; a small balance; a powder flask”). Such powder flasks initially looked like small weights; the sewing of the gazyr onto the front-garment began only later.
From Persian خال, ultimately from Arabic خال (ḵāl).
From Persian خاله (xâle), ultimately from Arabic خالة (ḵāla).
Equivalent to xalı (“a (large) carpet”) + -ça (diminutive suffix). Cognate with Kumyk халча (xalça).

From Old Anatolian Turkish قالی (qalı), from Persian خالی, although the direction of the borrowing is uncertain. Ultimately likely from Old Armenian Կարին (Karin), a city which was famed for its rugs.
Has been compared to Karakhanid قَلِنكْ (kalınğ, “dowry”), Karakhanid خُلِنكْ (xulınğ, “motley silk fabric imported from China”) and various words having the sense 'thick' (reflected in Azerbaijani qalın).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish خانم. Equivalent to xan + -ım (first person singular possessive suffix). Cognate with Turkish hanım. See also: bəyim.
Borrowed from Classical Persian خَانَگَاه (xānagāh), from خَانَه (xāna, “house”) + ـگَاه (-gāh).
Borrowed from Arabic خَانَقَاه (ḵānaqāh), from Classical Persian خَانَگَاه (xānagāh), from خَانَه (xāna, “house”) + ـگَاه (-gāh).
From Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (k¹g¹n¹), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kagan. Doublet of xan.
From Classical Persian خَرَابَه (xarāba), from Arabic خَرَابَة (ḵarāba).

From Armenian խաչ (xačʻ, “cross”), probably via Persian خاچ (xâč).
Izafet II compound of xaç + ata. Calque of Russian крёстный оте́ц (krjóstnyj otéc)

From Persian خیر (xeyr); ultimately from the same source as xeyir.

From Russian холоди́льник (xolodílʹnik). The letter i becoming an e appears to be a hypercorrection, since in Russian, the letter е (je) can be pronounced similarly to the letter и (i); see гепа́рд (gepárd), for example.

From Russian хозя́ин (xozjáin). Likely ultimately from Persian خواجه, in which case a doublet of qoca and xoca.
Borrowed from Persian خوشبخت (xošbaxt). By surface analysis, xoş + bəxt

Likely a calque of Persian خوش آمدن (xoš âmadan). In both languages, the construction is an impersonal one, where the liked object is in the ablative (in Persian expressed by the preposition از (“from”)), whereas the subject of liking is the possessor of خوش/xoş as expressed by a possessive suffix inflected for person and number and (in Azerbaijani) an optional free possessive pronoun. The formal predicate is the verb 'to come'.
Borrowed from Arabic خُصُوصًا (ḵuṣūṣan), adverbial accusative of خُصُوص (ḵuṣūṣ). By surface analysis, xüsus + -ən.
Onomatopoeic. Equivalent to xır + -ıltı (noun forming suffix).
From Persian خبردار (xabardâr). By surface analysis, xəbər + -dar.
Borrowed from Classical Persian خَجالَت (xajālat), a Pseudo-Arabism derived from the Arabic root خ ج ل (ḵ j l).

Borrowed from Persian غلبیر (ġalbir), from Arabic غِرْبَال (ḡirbāl).
Borrowed from Persian خمیر دندان (xamir dandân).
Borrowed from Classical Persian خسته (xasta). Cognate with Turkish hasta. The sense "fan, devotee" is a semantic loan from Russian боле́льщик (bolélʹščik).
From Persian خستهخانه (xaste-xâne). By surface analysis, xəstə (“sick”) + -xana.

From Persian خزینهدار. By surface analysis, xəzinə + -dar.

Borrowed from Classical Persian یا (yā, “either, or”).

Uzbek yot (“alien, foreign”), Turkmen ýat etc.
From yad (“foreign, alien”) + planet + -li. Possibly a calque of Russian иноплане́тный (inoplanétnyj).

mane (long or thick hair of a person's head or face)

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یل (yal, yel), from Proto-Common Turkic *yāl.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yālga- (“to lick”). Cognate with Turkish yalamak.

From Proto-Turkic *yala. Cognate with
Old Turkic [script needed] (jalγan, “false, fake”),
Turkish yalan (“lie”),
Bashkir ялған (yalğan, “false, fake”),
Kyrgyz жалған (“false, fake”),
Karachay-Balkar джалгъан (calğan, “fake, fictitious”),
Uzbek yolgʻon (“false, fake”),
Uyghur يالغان (yalghan, “lie; false, fake”),
Turkmen ýalan (“false, lie”),

Cognates
Cognate with Kazakh жалғаншы (jalğanšı), Kyrgyz жалганчы (jalgancı), Tatar ялганчы (yalğançı), Turkish yalancı, Turkmen ýalançy, Uzbek yolgʻonchi, Uyghur يالغانچى (yalghanchi).

glosses: to ride a horse without bridle, by holding its mane

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *yalŋuz, *yalïŋuz, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *yalïŋ (“lonely”), see there for more cognates. Doublet of yalqız. Related to Azerbaijani yalın (“naked, bare”), as in ayaqyalın (“barefoot”).
Inherited from Proto-Common Turkic *yalŋuz (“alone, lonely”). Doublet of yalnız (“only, merely”).
Ultimately a derivation from Proto-Turkic *yāl-. Cognate with Turkish yalvarmak.

From yalın (“bare, naked”) remodeled after göyərçin (“dove; dove-coloured”) and sarışın (“yellowish, blond”), where the suffix -çin/-şın signifies color nuances. Possibly a borrowing from Ottoman Turkish يالچين (yalçın, “smooth and bare”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (yamaj, “slope”). Cognate with Turkish yamaç.
From Proto-Turkic *yama- (“to patch”). Cognate with Turkish yamamak, Bashkir ямау (yamaw), see it for more cognates.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaman (“bad, wicked; sickness, inflammation”).

From yaman (“bad”) + yoz. The latter part is a contraction of the now archaic yovuz~yavuz~yavız, from Proto-Turkic *yabïŕ.
Uncontracted form yaman-yovuz~yaman-yavız does exist, too.

From Old Anatolian Turkish [Term?], from Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠮ (ǰam), whence also Mongolian зам (zam). Ultimately from Middle Chinese 站 (treamᴴ).
By surface analysis, yam + -çı.
from Proto-Turkic *yān (“side”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫум (śum), etc.
From Proto-Common Turkic. According to Dybo, the Proto-Turkic *yayŋak is reconstructable. Cognate with Turkish yanak, etc.
From yanaş + -ma. The sense “set” is a semantic loan from Russian подхо́д (podxód).

From Proto-Turkic *yan- (“to burn (intr.), blaze up”).Turkish yanmak, Crimean Tatar yanmaq (“to burn”), Bashkir яныу (yanıw, “to burn”), Chuvash ҫунма (śunma, “to burn, shine, worry, suffer”), Kazakh жану (januw, “to burn”), Kyrgyz жануу (januu, “to burn”), Turkmen ýanmak (“to be burnt”), Uzbek yonmoq (“to ignite, glow”), Yakut сандаар (sandaar, “to shine”) (< caus. *jan-tɨr-).
Internationalism; from Russian янва́рь (janvárʹ), from Latin Iānuārius.
Morphologically from yan + -ğın. Cognate with Turkish yangın, Turkmen ýangyn, Crimean Tatar yanğın, Uzbek yong'in, Tatar янгын (yanğın), Bashkir янғын (yanğın).
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaŋïl. Cognate with Turkish yanılmak.
From yanılt- + -mac. Cognate with Kyrgyz жаңылтмач (jaŋıltmac).
From Proto-Common Turkic *yapalak, from earlier *yapaku kulak 'furry ears'.

glosses: to stick or attach something onto a flat and vertical surface (such as flatbread dough onto the inner walls of a tandoor)

o.text: Morphologically from yapışmaq (“to stick, intransitive”) + -dır. Cognate with Chuvash ҫыпӑҫтар (śyp̬ăśtar), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *yapïĺč- (“to glue, stick to”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫыпӑҫ (śyp̬ăś) etc. See more cognates at Turkish yapışmak.
From yapış + -qan. Cognate with Turkish yapışkan.
Borrowed from Arabic يَاقُوت (yāqūt), ultimately from Ancient Greek ῠ̔ᾰ́κινθος (hŭắkinthos).
From Proto-Turkic *yara (“wound”), from which Azerbaijani yarıq with the same meaning is also derived.
From yaradıcı + -lıq. Senses likely influenced by Russian тво́рчество (tvórčestvo).
From Proto-Turkic *yara-. Cognate with Turkish yaramak, Chuvash ҫураҫ (śuraś, “to agree, consent”).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یراق (yaraq). By surface analysis, yara- (“to avail”) + -aq. Cognate with Turkish yarak.

Synonymous compound of yaraq + yasaq, the latter part being a loan from Middle Mongol ᠵᠡᠪᠰᠡᠭ (ǰebseg), cognate with Khalkha Mongolian зэвсэг (zevseg, “weapon”); not related to Azerbaijani yasaq (“prohibition”).
From Proto-Oghuz *yarasa, from Proto-Turkic *yar-, *yer-. Cognate with Gagauz, Turkish yarasa, Salar yarasan, dialectal Turkmen ýarasa, also related to Turkmen ýargānat.

From Proto-Turkic, probably a derivation of Proto-Turkic *yara- (“be good enough, be sufficient, be successful”), appended with the causative suffix -t.
Cognate with Turkish yaratmak,
Uzbek yaratmoq,
Kyrgyz жаратуу (jaratuu),
Kazakh жарату (jaratuw),
Bashkir яратыу (yaratıw),
Tatar яратучы (yaratuçı, “creator”),
Uyghur ياراتماق (yaratmaq).
Also compare Hungarian gyárt (“to manufacture”), a Turkic borrowing.
By surface analysis, yara- + -t.

According to most scholars, a derivation of Persian یار (yâr).
Alternatively, from a barely attested stem *yar-, in which case possibly related to *yara- (“to be good enough”). See Turkish yardım for Turkic cognates.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یارمق (yarmaq), from Proto-Turkic *yār- (“to split”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫур (śur), etc.

Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yapurgak (“leaf”). Developed through metathesis, compare Turkish yaprak. However, this phonological process has not occurred for all words in all dialects (see below). Cognate with Tatar яфрак (yafraq), etc.
From a derivation of Proto-Turkic *yal- (“name of different types of grass”). Cognate with Turkish yarpuz.
From Russian ярус (jarus); ultimately from Old Norse jarðhús.
From Proto-Turkic *yār. Cognate with Turkish yar, Chuvash ҫыр (śyr) etc.
From yar- (“split, cleave”) + -ım. Cognate to Proto-Turkic *yarïm.
From yarım (“half”) + ada (“island”). Possibly a calque of Russian полуостров (poluostrov, “peninsula”, literally “half-island”).
From yarım + fabrikat. Calque of Russian полуфабрика́т (polufabrikát).
From yarım + müdafiəçi. Calque of Russian полузащи́тник (poluzaščítnik).
From Old Anatolian Turkish یارین (yarïn), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yarïn.

Morphologically, from yarmaq (“to chop, cut, cleave, crack”) + -ış.
Cognates
Cognate with Karakhanid یَرِیشْ (yarïš, “contest, competition”); Turkish yarış,
Crimean Tatar yarış,
Kazakh жарыс (jarıs, “contest, competition”),
Kyrgyz жарыш (jarış, “running contest; competition”),
Southern Altai јарыш (ǰarïš, “running contest; horse race”),
Turkmen ýaryş (“contest, competition”), Tatar and
Bashkir ярыш (yarış, “contest, competition”),
Khakas чарыс (çarıs, “running contest; horse race”),
Tuvan чарыш (çarış, “running contest; competition”),
Yakut сырыс- (sïrïs-, “to race each other”).
From Proto-Turkic *yās (“damage, loss; shame”). Compare, however, also Arabic يَأْس (yaʔs, “despair”).

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یساغ (yasağ), from Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠰᠠᠭ (ǰasaɣ), whence Mongolian засаг (zasag, “rule, power; law”) and Mongolian засах (zasax, “to fix, repair”); ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *yasa- (“determine, govern; create”). Cognate with Turkish yasak (“prohibition”).
From Middle Mongol ᠵᠡᠪᠰᠡᠭ (ǰebseg), cognate with Mongolian зэвсэг (zevseg, “weapon”).
Ultimately from Middle Mongol 札撒兀勒 (zhásāwùlè /⁠⁠ǰasa'ul⁠/). Cognate with Mongolian засуул (zasuul).
From Proto-Common Turkic *yas- (“flat and broad”). Cognate with Turkish yassı, Turkmen ýasy, Uyghur يېسسى (yëssi), يېسە (yëse), etc.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaŕtuk (“pillow”), cognate with Turkish yastık, etc.

Borrowed from Classical Persian یَاسَمَن (yāsaman).
From Russian эта́п (etáp). Doublet of etap.
From yat- (“to sleep; to lie down”) + -aq. Cognate with Turkish yatak.
From yataq (“bed”) + -xana. Cognate with Turkish yatakhane.
From Proto-Turkic *yat-. Cognate with Turkish yatmak, Kazakh жату (jatuw, “to lie”), Uzbek yotmoq (“to lie”).
Borrowed from Turkish yatırım. By surface analysis, yatır- + -ım.
Morphologically from yat- (“to sleep”) + -ız + -dır. Two affixes with the same function have been used.

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yabgan (“unpleasant”).
Cognate with Turkish yavan.

From Proto-Turkic *yabaĺč.
Cognates
* Bashkir йыуаш (yıwaş)
* Crimean Tatar yavaş
* Gagauz yavaş
* Karachay-Balkar джууаш (cuuaş, “quiet,mild”)
* Karaim йуваш and йувас
* Kazakh жуас (juwas)
* Khakas чабас (çabas)
* Krymchak йуваш (“quiet, calm”)
* Nogai ювас (yuvas)
* Shor чобаш
* Southern Altai јобош (ǰoboš)
* Turkish yavaş
* Turkmen ýuwaş
* Tuvan чааш (çaaş), etc.

glosses: to catch, arrest, take hold of

o.text: From yaxa (“collar”) + -la. Literally, “to grab by the collar”.

From the earlier prevalent but now chiefly dialectal yayxalamaq, from yayxa- + -ala, for which compare Ottoman Turkish یایقامق (yayqamaq) and modern Turkish yıkamak. Ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *yāy- (“to shake”), and its older form *yāń-.
Related to yayxanmaq.
Morphologically yayxa- + -ntı. The stem yayxa- underwent assimilation to yaxa-, as also seen in yaxalamaq, from earlier yayxalamaq.

From Proto-Turkic *yak-
Cognate with Turkish yakmak, Chuvash ҫот (śot), etc.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یخشی (yaḫşı), which was borrowed from a non-Oghuz subbranch according to L. Johanson, from Proto-Common Turkic *yakšï, derivation of Proto-Turkic *yak- (“to draw near; to fit, to be well-suited”).

glosses: bow (a weapon used for shooting arrows)

o.text: From Proto-Turkic *yadag. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (yadaġ, “pedestrian, afoot”), Karakhanid [script needed] (yayaġ, “pedestrian, afoot”), Kazakh жаяу (jayaw, “pedestrian, afoot”), Turkish yaya (“pedestrian”), Uzbek yayov, etc.

glosses: to attach a spring; to fasten with a spring.

o.text: From yay + -laq. Cognate with Turkish yaylak, Kazakh жайлау (jaylaw), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *yaglïk (“kerchief, headscarf”). Cognate with Bashkir яулыҡ (yawlıq), see it for more cognates.
Borrowed from Turkish yazar. By surface analysis, yaz- (“to write”) + -ar.
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaŕ- (“to write”). Cognate with Turkish yazmak, Turkmen ýazmak, Crimean Tatar yazmaq, Chuvash ҫыр (śyr) etc.
From yazı (“writing”) + -lı or yazıl- (“to be written”) + -ı.

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یازق (yazuq), from Proto-Common Turkic *yāzuk, from Proto-Common Turkic *yāz- (“to err; to make a mistake; to miss out”).
Etymology notes
Cognate with Old Uyghur [script needed] (yazuk), Karakhanid یازُوکْ (yāzuq, “sin”), Kipchak yaxuc (yazuk), Ottoman Turkish یازیق (yazïq, “what a shame”), Gagauz yazık, Turkmen ýazyk (“sin, wrongdoing”), Crimean Tatar yazıq, Kumyk языкъ (yazıq, “pitiable”), Bashkir яҙыҡ (yaðıq, “sin, wrongdoing”), Tatar язык (yazıq, “sin”), Kazakh жазық (jazıq), Uzbek yoziq, Khakas чазых (çazıx), Southern Altai јазык (ǰazïk), Kyrgyz жазык (jazık). Compare also Yakut сыысхал (sïïsqal, “mistake”).
Has been compared to Chuvash ҫылӑх (śylăh, “sin”) which, if really cognate, would warrant a Proto-Turkic reconstruction; the Chuvash word is, however, rather from *yaŋïl, i.e. cognate with Azerbaijani yanlış, yanılmaq, etc.
The Old Turkic 𐰖𐰔‬‬𐰴 (yazïq, “plain, steppe”) is from *yaz- (“to spread out, to lay”), thus unrelated.
For the semantic development of 'sin' → 'sinful' → 'miserable' → 'poor, pitiable', compare the developments in the modern descendants of Old Norse synd (“sin”).

From yağ + -la.
Third sense is perhaps a semantic loan from Russian умасли́ть (umaslítʹ).

From Proto-Turkic *yag- (“to rain”).
Cognate with Turkish yağmak, Kazakh жауу (jawuw), Chuvash ҫу (śu), etc.

glosses: age (part of the duration of a being or thing between its beginning and any given time); years (of human age)

o.text: From Proto-Common Turkic *yāša-, a derivation from Proto-Turkic *yāĺ. By surface analysis, yaş (“year, age”) + -a.
By surface analysis, yaş + -ıd. Cognate with Turkish yaşıt. The function of the suffix is unclear.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یاشل (yaşıl), from Proto-Turkic *yāĺïl (“green”). Cognates include Turkish yeşil, Turkmen ýaşyl, Gagauz eşil.
From Proto-Turkic *yaĺ- (“to cover, close”). Cognate with Uzbek yashirmoq, Kazakh жасыру (jasıruw), Kyrgyz жашыруу (jaşıruu). Compare also Yakut сас (sas, “to hide”).
From Proto-Turkic *yẹt(t)i (“seven”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰃𐱅𐰃 (yeti, “seven”), Turkish yedi, etc.

Morphologically yeddi + -inci. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰃𐱅𐰨 (yetinči, “seventh”),
Turkish yedinci, Turkmen ýedinji, Kazakh жетінші (jetinši), etc.

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (yeke, “large”), from Middle Mongol ᠶᠡᠬᠡ (yeke), from Proto-Mongolic *jeke whence also Modern Mongolian их (ix, “great”).
Attested since the 13th century.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یل (yẹl), from Proto-Turkic *yẹl.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یلكن (yẹlken), from Proto-Turkic *yẹlken. Cognate with Turkish yelken.
Probably from yellən- (“to swing”) + -cək by contraction.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یللنمك (yẹllenmek). By surface analysis, yellə- + -n.
From a derivation of Proto-Common Turkic *yelpi-, *yalpï- (“to flap; to shake; fan”) .
From Proto-Turkic *yēm. By surface analysis, ye + -m.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yẹ̄miĺč (“vegetable, fruit”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫимӗҫ (śimĕś, “vegetable”), Hungarian gyümölcs (“fruit”), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *yẹ̄miĺčen. Cognate with Turkmen ýemşen (“hawthorn”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish یِمَكْ (yemäk), from Proto-Turkic *yē-. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰃𐰘𐰇 (y²iy²ü, “to eat”), Gagauz imää, Turkish yemek, Turkmen iýmek, Salar yegüsi etc.

From Proto-Turkic *yeŋe (“elder brother's wife”). Cognate with
Old Turkic [script needed] (yengä, “older male relative's wife”);
Turkish yenge (“wife of one's brother or uncle”), or, dialectally, "a woman that guides the bride on her wedding night",
Crimean Tatar yeñge,
Kazakh жеңге (jeŋge),
Kyrgyz жеңе (jeŋe), Southern Altai јеҥе (ǰeŋe),
Uyghur يەڭگە (yengge),
Yakut саҥас (saŋas, “older male relative's wife”)
Bashkir еңгә (yiñgä, “the wife of one's elder brother”).
Inherited from Early Old Oghuz يَنْكَجْ (yengeç), of unclear ultimate origin. Folk etymology derives it from yan (“side”) + -gəc, referring to the sideways walking of crabs.
From Proto-Turkic *yaŋï, *yeŋi (“new”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰖‬𐰭‬𐰃 (yaŋï).
From Ottoman Turkish یڭیچری. Equivalent to yeni + çəri.
From Proto-Turkic *yẹŋ- (“to win”). Cognate with Turkish yenmek and Kazakh жену (jenüw).
From Proto-Turkic *yAn-. Cognate with Turkish yine and yene, Kazakh және (jäne), Uzbek yana, Kyrgyz жана (jana), Bashkir йәнә (yänä), etc.
Borrowed from Russian епи́скоп (jepískop), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یر (yẹr), from Proto-Turkic *yẹr. Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰼 (yer), 𐰘𐰃𐰼 (yir), Turkish yer, Gagauz er, Turkmen ýer.
Present participle compound of yer (“earth”) + dəlmək (“to pierce, make a hole”). Calque of English earthscraper.
Present participle compound of yer (“ground”) + eş- (“to dig”).
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yorï-, *yüri- (“to walk”). Cognate with Turkish yürümek, see there for more.

Morphologically, from yeri- + -iş. Doublet of yürüş.
Cognates
* Bashkir йөрөш (yürüş, “walk”)
* Crimean Tatar yürüş (“walk; hike, march”),
* Gagauz örüyüş (“walk”),
* Karakalpak júris (“walk”),
* Kazakh жүріс (jüris, “motion, movement”),
* Krymchak йуруш (“gait”),
* Kyrgyz жүрүш (jürüş, “walk”),
* Kumyk юрюш (yurüş, “walk, gait, behaviour”),
* Nogai юрис (yuris, “walk”),
* Southern Altai јӱрӱш (ǰürüš, “walk”),
* Tatar йөреш (yöreş, “walk”),
* Turkish yeriş (“walk; fight, scuffle”) (Arpaçay, Kars; Erzurum), Turkish yürüyüş,
* Turkmen ýöriş (“walk”),
* Uyghur يۈرىش (yürish, “gate”),
* Uzbek yurish (“gate”)
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یرلو یرنده (yẹrlü yẹrinde). By surface analysis, yerli + yerində.
Izafet I compound of yer + tərpənmə. Possibly a calque of Russian землетрясение (zemletrjasenije, “earthquake”, literally “earth-shaking”).
Borrowed from Arabic أَسِير (ʔasīr). Doublet of əsir.
From Proto-Turkic *yẹt- (“to reach”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫит (śit).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یك (yẹg), Proto-Turkic *yẹg, cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰃𐰏 (y²ig²), Turkmen ýeg, Turkish yey, yeğ, possibly with Chuvash ҫи (śi, “up, upper”).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یینی (yeyni, “lightweight”), یكول (yeŋül), from Proto-Turkic *yeŋil. Cognate with Turkish yeğni, Gagauz ilin.

From Proto-Turkic *yeŕne (“son-in-law, sister's husband”).
Cognate with Tatar җизни (cizni), Bashkir еҙнә (yiðnä), Kazakh жезде (jezde), Chuvash йысна (jysna).
From Russian я́щик (jáščik), ultimately derived from Old Norse askr.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ایه (eye, iye), from Proto-Turkic *idi. Compare Turkmen eýe, Turkish iye, Kazakh ие (iye), etc.
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yōl. Cognate with Turkish yol, Chuvash ҫул (śul), etc.
Morphologically yol (“road”) + -daş (“fellow, sharer”). Cognate with Kipchak یولداش (“travelling companion”).

From Proto-Turkic *yol-. Cognate with Chuvash ҫӑл (śăl), Turkish yolmak, Uyghur يۇلماق (yulmaq), Yakut сулуй (suluy).
Unrelated to Azerbaijani yol (“road”), which is derived from *yōl.

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yorïnčga.
Cognates
Cognate with Ottoman Turkish یونجه (yonca),
Old Turkic [script needed] (yorınçga, yorunçga),
Azerbaijani yonca,
Gagauz yonca,
Crimean Tatar yonca,
Nogai йорынша (yorınşa),
Turkmen ýorunja, Karaim yonca, Urum yonca,
Karakalpak jońıshqa, Krymchak yonca,
Kyrgyz жоңгучка (joŋgucka), etc.
Probably from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (yorı-, “to walk”). Alternatively, a regular derivation from yor- (“to tire”) + -ul, ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *yor-.

From Proto-Turkic *yor(ɨ)- (“to walk”).
Cognate with Turkish yorga, Turkmen ýorga, Kazakh жорға (jorğa), Kyrgyz жорго (jorgo), Uzbek yoʻrgʻa, Bashkir юрға (yorğa), Yakut дьоруо (joruo).
Inherited from Proto-Turkic *jogurgan (“blanket”). Analyzable as yor + -ğan. See also Kyrgyz жууркан (juurkan), Southern Altai јууркан (ǰuurkan) and Turkish yorgan.
From Proto-Turkic *yabĺan (“wormwood”). Cognate with Turkish yavşan, Turkmen ýowşan, Tuvan чашпан (çaşpan), Kazakh жусан (juwsan).
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yōk (“there is not”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰖𐰸 (yok), Turkish yok etc.

From yox + -al.
Cognates
* Kazakh жоғалу (joğaluw, “to get lost”)
* Kyrgyz жоголуу (jogoluu, “to disappear, to get lost”)
* Uzbek yoʻqolmoq (“get lost”)
* Uyghur يوقالماق (yoqalmaq, “to get lost, disappear”)
* Turkish yoğalmak (“to disappear”)
* Turkmen ýogalmak (“to disappear, die”)

Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یوخیسه (yoḫısa). Compare Turkish yoksa (“otherwise”), Turkmen ýogsa (“otherwise, or else”), Turkmen ýogsam (“otherwise”). Equivalent to yox (“no; there is not”) + isə.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یوقش (yokuş, “rise, slope”), from a derivation of Proto-Turkic *yok (“up, above; hill”). Cognate with Turkish yokuş.

From Proto-Turkic *yor- (“to interpret”). Cognate with Turkish yormak (“interpret”), Turkmen ýormak (“to foretell, interpret”), Kyrgyz жоруу (joruu, “to interpret”), Kazakh жору (joruw, “to interpret”).
The development of the coda-final /z/ remains unclear. Possibilities include an expected development of the Proto-Turkic /*ŕ/, which was unexpectedly turned into /r/ instead of /z/ in all other cognates (as in reflexes of *köŕ- (“to see”)); or development of the variant *yod-, as reflected in dialectal Turkish yoymak, Uzbek yoʻymoq and joʻymoq.
Possibly a derivation of Proto-Common Turkic *yog- (“to become denser, to thicken”).
From Proto-Turkic *yugur-. Cognate with Turkish yoğurmak, Chuvash ҫӑр (śăr).

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yogrut (“curdled, coagulated milk”), from *yogur- (“to knead, to fluff up, to condense”) *-ut. Equivalent to yoğur- (“to knead”) + -d.
cognates
Cognate with Old Uyghur 𐽶𐽳𐽲𐽾𐽳𐾀 (yogrut, “yogurt”), Turkish yoğurt, Kyrgyz жуурат (juurat), and Yakut суорат (suorat).
From Proto-Turkic *yuba- (“to be late, to delay; to console, to comfort”).
From Arabic عَلَف (ʕalaf). Doublet of alaf.

glosses: to wash away (often used as a converb, followed by aparmaq (“to carry away”))
yarn ball, clew (of thread), ball of wool

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish یومق (yumaq), from Proto-Turkic *yu(b)- (“to wash”). Cognate with Turkish yumak, Chuvash ҫу (śu) etc.
Derived from Proto-Turkic *yum (“round”), whence also yumru, and perhaps also yumurta. Cognate with Turkish yumak. See there for more cognates.
From Proto-Turkic *yum-, *yüm- (“to close (eyes, mouth)”). See more at Turkish yummak.
From Russian ю́мор (júmor), from English humour.
From Proto-Turkic *yum (“round”). Possibly related to Azerbaijani yumruq (“fist”) and Azerbaijani yumurta (“egg”).
From Proto-Turkic *yum (“round”) or Proto-Turkic *yum- (“to close”). See more at Turkish yumruk.
From Proto-Turkic *yïm-ĺča-k (“soft, mild”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰘𐰢𐱁𐰴 (yïmšaq), Turkish yumuşak, Crimean Tatar yımşaq, yumşaq, etc.
Ultimately a calque of English soft power.

Inherited from Proto-Turkic *yuŋ.
Cognates
Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (yüŋ), Turkish yün, Turkmen ýüň, Tatar йон (yon), Kazakh жүн (jün), Kyrgyz жүн (jün), Uzbek jun, Bashkir йөн (yün), Tuvan чүң (çüñ) Nogai юн (yun), Crimean Tatar yün, Khakas нӱң (nüñ), Karachay-Balkar джюн (cün), Kumyk юн (yun), Chagatai [script needed] (yüŋ), Southern Altai јуҥ (ǰuŋ) / јум (ǰum), Uyghur يۇڭ (yung).
From Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place, camping-site”). Cognate with Chuvash ҫорт (śort), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *uya. Cognate with Chuvash йӑва (jăva).
From yuva + -cıq. The sense 'outlet' is a partial calque of Russian гнездо́ (gnezdó, “nest; wall socket”).
From Old Anatolian Turkish یوقارو (yuqaru), from Proto-Common Turkic *yok-karï (“upper; upward”), from Proto-Turkic *yok.

From metatheses of the early Azerbaijani uyxu, uyqu or from an apheresis of Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (uyuχu); ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ūdï-ku, a derivation of Proto-Turkic *ūdï- (“to sleep”).

From yön + -lü.
Cognates
* Bashkir юнле (yonli, “sensible; decent; worthy, suitable”)
* Karakalpak jónli (“worthwhile, decent; right, fair”)
* Tatar юньле (yünle, “decent, honest; smart, intelligent; good, worthy, suitable”)
* Turkish yönlü (“suitable, good, correct, appropriate”) (dialectal, Burdur, Sivas, Niğde, Konya, Antalya)
Perhaps from the verb Proto-Turkic *yörge- (“wrap, swathe”); the synonymous çevrə and دكره are derived from verbs meaning to "turn, rotate, topple".
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الجُمْعَة (yawm al-jumʕa).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الاِثْنَيْن (yawm al-iṯnayn).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الخَمِيس (yawm al-ḵamīs).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الأَحَد (yawm al-ʔaḥad).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الأَرْبَعَاء (yawm al-ʔarbaʕāʔ).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم الثُّلَاثَاء (yawm aṯ-ṯulāṯāʔ).
Borrowed from Arabic يَوْم السَّبْت (yawm as-sabt).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish اوكش (/⁠üküş, ügüş⁠/), from Proto-Turkic *üküĺ. Cognate with Bulgar اَكِل.
From Proto-Turkic *yǖk (“load; to load, carry”). Cognate to Turkish yük, Chuvash ҫӑк (śăk), Kazakh жүк (jük), Southern Altai јӱк (ǰük, “load, cargo, burden”), etc.
By surface analysis, yük + -lə. The computing senses are a semantic loan from Russian загружать (zagružatʹ).

From Arabic زَرَافَة (zarāfa), ultimately from Classical Persian زرناپا.
Borrowed from Persian زحمتکش (zahmatkeš), equivalent to zəhmət (“labour; effort; suffering; troubles”) + -keş.
From Classical Persian زهر مار (“snake venom”). Cognate with Armenian զահրմար (zahrmar).

Borrowed from Persian زنجبیل (zanjabil), زنجفیل (zanjafil), from Sanskrit शृङ्गवेर (śṛṅgavera). Ultimately from Old Tamil.

From Persian سنگین (sangin, “heavy”), possibly via Ottoman Turkish زنگین (zengin). Doublet of səngin.

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (ögey), from Proto-Turkic *ögey, cognate with Turkish üvey.
In Azerbaijani, non-initial /-g-/ has evolved to /-j-/, whereas in Turkish it has evolved to /-v-/, compare Turkish dövmek vs. Azerbaijani döymək, both from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (dögmek, “to beat”); Turkish sövmek vs. Azerbaijani söymək, both from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (sögmek, “to swear”). Turkish üvey (“step-”) therefore demonstrates a regular phonological development, while the Azerbaijani term unexpectedly preserves the intervocalic /-g-/ instead of the expected /-j-/, which would yield *öyey.

From Persian علاقهدار. By surface analysis, əlaqə + -dar.

From əl (“hand”) + çat- (“reach”) + -ım. Compare əlçatan. Attested since 2016.
From Proto-Turkic *elgek (“sieve”). By surface analysis, ələ- + -ik.
Izafet II compound of əmanət + kassa. Calque of Russian сберега́тельная ка́сса (sberegátelʹnaja kássa).

From Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (emcek). Ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *em- (“to suck”), whence also əmmək (“to suck”) and əmizdirmək (“to breastfeed”). Cognate with Turkish emcik (“breast”), Turkmen emjek (“breast, udder”), Uzbek emchak (“udder”), Uyghur ئەمچەك (emchek, “breast, udder”), Chuvash ӗм (ĕm, “to suck”), etc.
From Proto-Turkic *yem-kek. Cognate with Turkish imik, Kazakh еңбек (eŋbek), etc.
From Proto-Turkic․ Cognate with Turkish emlik (“suckling animal or infant”).
From Proto-Turkic *em- (“to suck”). Cognate with Chuvash ӗм (ĕm).

From Proto-Turkic *emgek
Cognates
Cognate with Turkish emek (“labour, toil”), Turkmen emgenmek (“to work hard, to suffer”), Kazakh еңбек (eŋbek, “labour”), Uyghur ئەمگەك (emgek, “labour, toil”), Bashkir имгәк (emgäk, “labour, burden”), Tatar имгәк (imgäk, “burden, cripple”), Yakut эмэх (emeq, “rotten”), Chuvash амак (amak, “illness”). According to Starostin, not cognate with Turkish emeklemek (“to crawl”)

Izafet II compound of əmək + mühacir.
Likely a calque of Russian трудово́й мигра́нт (trudovój migránt).
From əmək + -dar. Compare Ottoman Turkish امكدار (emekdâr). Compare Russian заслу́женный (zaslúžennyj).
Ultimately from Arabic عَمَل (ʕamal). Some senses may be derived from Arabic أَمَل (ʔamal).
From əməl + -li. The word əməl has connotations of intentional and consequential work, so the current senses evolved from something like "having meaningful consequences, working, functioning".
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish اك (äŋ). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰭 (ŋ /⁠eŋ⁠/), Uzbek eng, Kyrgyz эң (eŋ), Turkish en.

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish انكنار (enginar, inginar, “artichoke”), from Greek αγκινάρα (agkinára).

From Arabic عَقْل (ʕaql). Doublet of ağıl.
From Arabic أَقْرِبَاء (ʔaqribāʔ), plural of قَرِيب (qarīb).
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ار (er), from Proto-Turkic *ēr.

Borrowed from Arabic أَرْبَاب (ʔarbāb), plural of رَبّ (rabb).
Calque of Russian пла́вленый сыр (plávlenyj syr).
From Proto-Turkic *ẹri-. Cognate with Turkish erimek.
From Proto-Turkic *ar- (“weft, woof; warp”), whence also Azerbaijani arğac (“weft, woof”).

o.text: Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ارك (erk), from Proto-Turkic *erk. Compare Turkish erk.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ارك (erk), from Persian ارک, alternative form of ارگ.
From Arabic أَرْزَاق (ʔarzāq), plural of Arabic رِزْق (rizq). Ultimately from Middle Persian 𐭫𐭥𐭰𐭩𐭪 (rōzīg, “sustenance, daily bread”). Compare Turkish erzak.
From Arabic عَرَفَة (ʕarafa). See Turkish arife.
Inherited from Old Anatolian Turkish ارن (ẹren, eren), from Proto-Turkic *ēren, the irregular plural of Proto-Turkic *ēr (“man”). Cognate with Kazakh ерен (eren).
Ultimately from Arabic السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (as-salāmu ʕalaykum, “may peace be upon you”).
From Arabic ء س ر (ʔ s r, root); compare Turkish esaret.
Borrowed from Arabic أَسَاسًا (ʔasāsan), adverbial accusative of أَسَاس (ʔasās). By surface analysis, əsas + -ən.
